It is nearly fifty years ago since I was taught, as a schoolboy, that our word Hudson's Bay was always spelled with the ' s,' whereas the United States\n\nriver Hudson was spelled without the ' s '. I think that is a very good reason, if no ether existed, why we should adhere to the English method of spelling this word. It is a different word, and, however much we may admire modern improvements in spelling, we cannot change the name of the great company which had its charter now nearly 250 years ago, and which has made famous the world over the name Hudson's Bay. I think the very circumstance that we have our own expression, while the United States have theirs, that it is the English language we speak, and, therefore, that _we ought to look to England for our standards of orthography and geography, affords in itself reason enough why, in an official proceeding of this character, we ought to adhere to the expression Hudson's Bay, whatever newspapers and whatever other peojde may do about it."]

As my hon. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir bred-erick Borden) is now present, I would invite my hon. friend from St. Anne Division, Montreal (Mr. Doherty) to repeat in his presence the objections vvhich he voiced on a previous occasion to the selection of the site for the new Montreal barracks, the particulars of which I was not able to give.
Montreal, new barracks, $100,000.

When this item came up on the two previous occasions we understood from the Minister of Public Works that the barracks were to be constructed at Longueuil, and that one of the important purposes of this barracks was to place a unit of the permanent force there, and to provide a military school for the benefit of the Montreal district. I inquired then whether the officers who take an active interest in militia matters in Montreal had been consulted, and had approved of the location of these barracks at Montreal or what their judgment had been. For myself, while I do not undertake to pronounce a judgment on that matter, I did venture to point out that a military school situated so far away from the residences of the majority of the young men who would in all probability attend this school, was open to some objection, that it was a place difficult of access, and would hardly meet the want that has been felt in Montreal. If 1 am not mistaken, it has been found that the military school situated at St. Johns does not afford the oportunity that-was expected for the young men, who I am sure we would all be glad to see taking an active part in the operations of our militia, and who we want to see afford-

The situation of the school at St. Johns was found to be such as to prevent a large number of young men taking advantage of it, inasmuch as they are all engaged in business activities, and it is impossible for them, without great inconvenience and considerable loss, to absent themselves from the city. Now to overcome that objection it was suggested that we should have a military school in Montreal, but a military school at Longueuil can hardly be called a military school in Montreal. Individually, I am not familiar with the precise site on which it is proposed to erect these barracks, but I do know that the access from different portions of Montreal, I think I may say from those portions where the majority of those who want to use the school would come from, is not convenient or easy. If this school is to be available for the class of young men who are to attend it, I think it would be important that its courses should take the form of evening instruction, and if they do take that form, it will be exceedingly difficult, in many cases impossible for young men to go over to Longueuil early enough in the evening to have any reasonable time to devote to their lessons and get back home again at a reasonable hour. I do not oppose the erection of the barracks, but I am pointing out what I think is desirable, namely, that the minister should take the judgment of those officers in the Montreal district who know the needs and requirements of the class of young men whd, are to attend this school.

speakeroldname: Sir FREDERICK BORDEN (Minister of Militia and Defence).
speechtext:
I think the points of view presented by my hon. friend from St. Anne (Mr. Doherty) are entitled to the greatest possible consideration, ^and they have not escaped the consideration of the department. I can say that the officers of the garrison of Montreal, or perhaps more important still, the military district of Montreal, have been consulted, some of them at any rate, about this matter. As a matter of fact, they are interested in the establishment of a military school at Montreal, and have been for a long time I have had an opportunity of discussing the matter with a good many of the more prominent men, and I will say at once that while they do not all approve of the location at this point-there is no one place perhaps in the city of Montreal on which they would all agree-I think, however, I can safely say that in a general way the officers of the city of Montreal, and of the military district of Montreal, will be satisfied with this location. The difficulty of accessibility that my hon. friend has referred to is an important one. But the same difficulty would exist if, for instance, the school had been located at Pointe aux
Trembles, which was one of the places talked of. We own a large rifle range at Pointe aux Trembles, a few miles below the city of Montreal, although it may now be within the eitv limits.
That was talked of, and the present proposal is more agreeable to the officers generally, as far as I know, than the location at Pointe Aux Trembles would be. Then there was a suggestion as to Lachine, another point some distance to the westward of the centre of the city, quite as far away as the present proposed location. That proposal would have been as good as the present proposal but no better. So, upon the whole, even from the point of view of accessibility I think the present location is fairly satisfactory. Accessibility will be measured by time. How long does it take from a given point, the post office, or some central point in the city of Montreal to get to a given place? I understand that by way of the Victoria bridge at all times of the year, and by crossing the river by ferry in certain seasons of the year, the time occupied in going from the centre of Montreal to Longueuil is only a few minutes, and that the tendency is towards improvement in that regard. There is the Southern Counties railway, and there is the street railway giving direct accommodation with the centre of Montreal-better communication than there is with our rifle ranges at Pointe Aux Trembles. I think there is no serious difficulty on that ground. As far as officers outside of the city are concerned, it cannot make any difference to them and these military depots are of quite as much importance to the country militia as to the city militia.
As to evening schools and that sort of thing, I do not know what the course of instruction would ibe, but it would always be easy for us to arrange a course of instruction at hours which would suit professional and business men in the city, and an effort will be made to do that wherever the location may be. We had also to consider, Mr. Chairman, another matter of importance, and that is the question of expense. The government own this land. It was owned by the British war office, and it was handed over to the Canadian government at the time of confederation. It is a block of land between 100 and 200 acres in extent and, -as a matter of fact, it is costing Canada not one single dollar as against the problem we had before us of purchasing between 100 and 200 acres of land in the city of Montreal, or near Montreal at a cost of $300,000 or $400,000, and perhaps $1,000,000. It seemed to me that that was a point that could not be disregarded. It is a matter of very considerable consequence, and I felt that a very difficult problem had been solved when I found this land practically waiting for us, and I thought I was acting in the public interest

as well as in the interest of the militia, to have adopted it as a site for our barracks at Montreal.
I may say that in addition to my own judgment I consulted the best military authorities we had. I consulted General Sir Percy Lake, who was here at that time, and he entirely approved, and I think I may say that it is the unanimous opinion of the Militia Council, and of the best authorities here and in Montreal that we should have pursued the course we have.
I think that perhaps covers the points raised, but I understand my hon. friend from Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Hughes) to raise a question as to the overflow of certain portions of this land at certain times when the river is high, and as to the unsanitary conditions which might arise therefrom. It is a most important question, and it has received and is receiving the careful consideration of the department. I believe that with a very slight expenditure of money in erecting a dyke all these difficulties of overflow can be met. There is only a small portion of the land which has ever overflowed at any time, and that can be protected by a proper dyke as is done at many points on the other side of the river about Montreal itself. As to the sanitary conditions, I am informed that the greatest difficulty is with regard to the water, tout, of course that is a problem which can be solved and must be solved. As to the question of getting rid of sewage there is a difficulty, but we are able to solve that difficulty, and it will toe done in accordance with the most up to date principles governing matters of hygiene.

I desire, to correct a mistake which has been made by several hon. gentlemen who have spoken on this question. They speak of the site of the barracks as being in Longueuil. For instance, T heard my hon. friend from St. Anne (Mr. Doherty) referring to it in that way. It should have been referred to as Montreal South. Montreal South is a distinct municipality, and I have received two or three letters from gentlemen protesting against it being confused with Longueuil. They do not want it to be called Longueuil, they want it to be called Montreal South because it is a distinct and a very, active municipality. As regards the transportation question, as the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Frederick Borden) has just said, access to it is easy enough now by any of the three routes available-the steam railway, the electric railway, and the ferry boat. Unless you located the site in the very city of Montreal you could not get a better place or one more quickly accessible than the site of Montreal South. If you desired to locate at Pointe Aux Trembles or any other place outside of Montreal you would have to go a long distance Sir FREDERICK BORDEN.
out before you could get as large a space as you get at Montreal South. You cannot get a more healthy place than Montreal South. It is on a higher level than the city of Montreal unless you get up on the mountain, it is higher than Longueuil, and it has a magnificent water-power to get water from. I do not think there is a place in the province of Quebec healthier than Longueuil and Montreal South. The water which flows on the south side of the 'St. Lawrence is freer from impurity than the water in the other portions of the St. Lawrence in the vicinity of Montreal. The minister has said truly that the question of expense is a very important one. The government own 180 acres of land there which they can get for nothing, which has been there doing nothing and giving no revenue at all. If they bought the same quantity of land somewhere around the city of Montreal I do not think they could get it for less than $300,000.

Yes, and that is a very important consideration. I would point out to my hon. friend (Mr. Doherty), that the men who will use that school do not all come from the city of Montreal, but live in the military district. I do not think the government could have made a better choice.
Is it of convenient access for the officers and men living in the city of Montreal P
Certainly. There are four ways to get there: an electric railway service every 15 minutes, a steam railway, a ferry boat, and in winter the ice bridge.

I must apologize most profoundly and most humbly to the outraged inhabitants of Alontreal South, that I "should have been guilty of describing them as citizens of Longueuil, I had thought that Longueuil was a fairly goed, an eminent name in this country, but as a good Montrealer, 1 can sympathize with the desire- of all Canadians to connect themselves with the name of that great city. I trust my hon. friend (Mr. Geof-frion), will convey to his outraged constituents my humble apology. I would plead by way of mitigation that the Alinister of Public Works told me the barracks was to be built in Longueuil.

I said the barrracks was to be built at Tete du Pont, and my hon. friend (Air. Doherty), should know where that is.
Air. DOHERTYi Well, perhaps the residents of the city of Alontreal South would rather be described as living at Tete du Pont than at Longueuil. Be that as it may, I would not venture to put my judgment

against that of the high military authorities who are said to have pronounced in favour of this location. I do not want to make any invidious comparison, hut I think it will have to be conceded that the greater number of those who will use the school, live in the city of Montreal, and from that point of view, it is not unreasonable to urge that the convenience of the greater number should be a major consideration in this matter. After all, there is not much object in having a school if you do not have the scholars, and if our militia is to be what we desire, then we should endeavour to put at the disposal of these patriotic young men who devote their time and energy to the service of their country, every facility for qualifying themselves in the best manner. There is no doubt that the question of economy is also important, and it has been pointed out that this land now belongs to the Crown, and that it would cost a great deal of money to purchase property in Montreal. But, Montreal is fairly large even without going to Pointe aux Trembles or Lachine, and w7ithin its municipal area there are to be found properties of very varying value. If the purpose to be served can only be properly served by putting the school in tfie city of Montreal, then the country ought to be willing to spend the monev. To build an establishment of this sort in a place where it will not serve its purpose, simplv because you can build it cheaply, is like going to a bargain counter to buy things you don t want, simply because you get them under the regular price. Certain!'-if we cannot get the school to serve its purpose then we had better save our money.
Does the hon gentleman want the school to be built within the limits of the city of Montreal ?	.

My desire is that the school should he built in a place sufficiently accessible to the majority of those who will use it so as to produce the best possible results. I do not say that it is absolutely necessary that it should be within the limits of the city, but you can get outside the city limits without going across the St. Lawrence river. True, as we have been told, there is a railway, a ferry boat, and a tramway running to the south shcq-e, but the ferry boat starts from the extreme end of the city which makes it * 3 ^on" journey for the residents of bt. Anne, or St. Antoine, or the North End, and, the feny boat only runs at eer-tam intervals. Then, the ferry runs from Montreal to the very much despised Long-ueuil, and after you get to Longueuil, you are still quite a distance from Montreal South I doubt very much if a large mini-her of the officers and men could sret from
their residences to the ferry and across the river in less than an hour or an hour and a quarter. As to the steam railway, I would suppose that the trains are not run at hours which would enable those attending the night school to get from the city to the school and return the same evening. I am informed by those who use the tramway, that at certain hours of the day, (in the evening particularly), the tramway runs once every 40 minutes, and if one car is missed, you have to wait 40 minutes for another, which of course, would be an obstacle to attending the evening school by that means of access. On the whole, it appears to me that the location of the school would be highly inconvenient for a large number of the young men, unless they should be prepared to sacrifice their time at the occupations by which they earn their livelihod. I understand the minister to say that the officers of the district, so far as he consulted them, were not agreed on any one site in Montreal, and I would be glad to know if they did not at least agree that it would be desirable to have some site in Montreal or in the^ immediate vicinity of the city. Is the minister aware that the public press in Montreal has spoken upon this subject and that ' La Presse,' a newspaper which certainly is not unfriendly to the present administration, but which has given them a very consistent support, had an article on this subject since the matter came up in this House, in which it pointed out briefly, but with great force, the objections I had been making. Furthermore, that newspaper'takes the responsibility of saying that the place is in a most doubtful condition from the point of view of health and the further responsibility, which 1 would not take, of saying that the officers or men connected with the permanent force, condemn the site as being in most doubtful sanitary condition. This respond sible journal, I presume after inquiry, has felt justified in making these statements, and I need not say that they have not been inspired by me. The fact that this paper takes the responsibility of making these statements, should furnish ground "for the minister to at least, promise that the grounds for these assertions shall be looked into, and that it shall be made quite certain that from the point of view of health, there is no objection to the site chosen. '

I will repeat what I have said in regard to the latter point: all questions relating to water supply and sanitation have received, are receiving and will receive most careful consideration. I do not think there is any difficulty with reference to these particular points. As to the question of accessibility and the view which officers in Mont-

real take of the site, several of the prominent senior officers of Montreal have told me that they prefer this site to some sites within the city of Montreal which have been mentioned. As to the means of getting to the place and the statement that there is only one car in 40 minutes, these are growing times, and I am rather inclined to think that when the military barracks and school are situated at Montreal South there may be a car once in every 20 minutes, or perhaps once in every 10 minutes. So I do not think that is a very serious difficulty.
As to the relative numbers of officers and non-commissioned officers who require facilities for teaching or training living in the city of Montreal and in the country, 1 think a very much larger number live in the country and therefore if we satisfy the outside portion of the militia we are accomplishing a good deal. The fullest steps will be taken to consult the convenience of officers and non-commissioned officers residing in Montreal. I cannot see why evening classes might not be held at the new school at Montreal South; there will be no difficulty in getting there before 8 o'clock or 7.30, and in getting home after 10, probably 25 or 30 minutes would be all that would be necessary to get from Montreal to school. Then it is quite common to hold classes in the great central drill hall in Montreal, and there is no reason why a detachment of instructors should not to be sent into the city at any time to suit the convenience of any officers who find it inconvenient to go to the barracks. So, taking it for all in all, I think this will be found to be an entirely satisfactory solution of a very difficult problem, one of the most difficult I have had to contend with since I became Minister of Militia. We have been talking about establishing this school at Montreal for over 14 years, and I am looking forward with a great deal of pleasure to the day when my hon. friend will have these buildings constructed and this school and barracks successfully established.

Last year two or three officers wrote me concerning this proposed site. Their objections were first the inaccessibility of the site, and second, the condition of the ground. It was pointed out by these gentlemen that part of the ground is very low and that part of it is a sticky clay, so that on dewy mornings, unless it were well drained, it would be a rather unfavourable ground on which to drill. I have made inquiries from some of the gentlemen representing that part of the country and they tell me that that condition extends only a short distance along the river bank and that the ground is higher and more sandy further back.
That is true, it is very high ground, most of it.

I happen to be acquainted with the topography of that place, and I think there is some misunderstanding. Montreal South is a thriving suburb and the land just near the St. Lawrence is a rather favourable site, but it gets lower as you go back, and if the property in question is somewhat remote from the river there will be considerable expense in draining it. Why has the site been changed? Because at one time the government had decided practically upon a different and to my mind a very much more convenient site. Why the department should have left that site aside in order to take one much less convenient, one would like to know.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Does my hon. friend say there was a site selected by the government before this one?

The government at one time selected a site on the western slope of the mountaiu, and it is absurd to talk of a price of $400,000 or $500,000 for that site, because that property was sold lately for $150,000 and could have been bought for less when the government had it in view. If you calculate what it will cost to build at Montreal South on account of the sanitary condition of the ground there, you will find that this government, however desirous it may be to economize, might have spent $150,000 in buying the site on the slope of the mountain and still have saved money. It is a matter of almost public notoriety that the military officers in Montreal highly approved of that site. I understood that the minister himself (Sir Frederick Borden) had visited it and pronounced it unequalled.
What place?
The site chosen at North-mount, not very far from the Hunt Club.
I never chose it.
Well, we thought it was a sure thing because we heard that the order in council had been passed.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: There never was such an order in council passed
Does my hon. friend deny that there was a question of this site?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: There was question of several sites, but there never was any order in council passed selecting that site.

That may be, but it was rumoured in Montreal that the matter had been put through with the approval of the Governor General. The site I refer to is situated within a few minutes of every part

of the city. Every car leaves there and you can get there ior 4 cents at any hour of the day or night.
So every car leaves there with a transfer.
When you embark on this new railway, the Montreal and Southern railway, and get to the other side, my hon. friend knows there is still a great distance to go before vou reach this place.
The electric road runs right alongside this property.
At any rate, it is quite a distance to reach from the ferry, or the starting point of this new electric road.
You can start from McGill street, in the centre of the city.
How often does my hon. friend go there?
I go there every week and I take the cars on McGill street,

My hon. friend knows perfectly well that you have to get over there before you can take the railway, and you do not get a transfer. You have to go to the foot of McGill street and there take the car, and it takes you 40 minutes to get to Longueuil. I am not aware what the fare is.
It is 5 cents right to the grounds, and there is a car every 3 minutes, not every 40 minutes.
Is my hon. friend quite sure the fare is only 5 cents?
Quite sure.

It seems to me impossible to compare the two places. For the people of the city-and those who will avail themselves of the school will mostly come from the city-and for students from the country it would be vastly more convenient to have the site within the limits of the city than on the outside. I am not versed in strategy, but perhaps my hon. friend from Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Hughes) could give us some pointers on that; but I should think that in the case of war it would be better to have the school on the top of a mountain than on low ground on the other side of the river and close to the United States. Of course, I am not talking from a naval point of view.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: It would have this advantage, that a navy could get there.

By the time we shall have done the sanitary work required there and other necessary expenditures, we shall have expended more than one-half of what we could have bought this place for on the slope of the mountain. We understood at the time that experts from the department, ' 100
high up in the military organization, had visited that site at Northmount and had unanimously recommended it. The department has largely increased its expenditure. We are spending over $7,000,000 this year and our expenditure will soon be up to $10,000,000, as compared with the $1,200,000 which we expended some years ago.
In what riding is Northmount?
It is just alongside the riding of my hon. friend.
There are many ridings alongside of mine. It is alongside the riding of the hon. gentleman.

My hon. friend is altogether too cunning. He knows very well where it is, and must not imagine that in a matter of this kind it is anxiety to have the military school in the county of Jacques Cartier which leads me to make these observations. I am very much interested in Montreal South, as I am a land owner there, and also very much interested in the progress of Montreal, and I certainly did not dream it was in the interests of the county of Jacques Cartier that I supported the very reasonable view taken by the hon. member for St. Anne (Mr. Doherty).

There never was any lot of land chosen by the department as a location for a military school in Montreal. There was a lot at Lachine, and I do not know whether it is this one to which my hon. friend refers.
No, to Northmount, which is on the western slope of the mountain.

There was a lot, part of the way up the mountain which I visited myself at one time, but which the general officer then, General Lake, told me was altogether too small and would not suit the purpose at all. I went and visited the lot myself, and it seemed to me not large enough. It was some 50 to 60 acres at the most, and would have cost over $200,000.
It has just been sold to a religious order for $150,000, and property has considerably advanced.

I am speaking of the price put upon it at that time. It seemed to me altogether beyond a reasonable price-I do not mean for the land, but to be paid by this department for that quantity of land. I wish to emphasize the point that there never was a lot of land in Montreal or anywhere else selected for this purpose until we had decided upon this.
How is this property situated for rifle ranges?
It is exactly opposite the Pointe aux (Trembles rifle range which point is accessible by ferry, and the rifle ranges will answer the purposes of the permanent force there perfectly well.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I cannot refrain from expressing my gratification at finding that my hon. friend from Jacques1 Cartier (Mr. Monk) is showing himself more and more in favour of military and naval expenditure -provided that the expenditure be made in his own county. He did not so express it, but the lot of land he had in mind when he spoke a few minutes ago is situated in his county, and he was. willing to have military expenditure made there. Perhaps my hon. friend's attitude in opposition to military expenditure might be pleaded as justifying our refusal to select the site to which he refers-it might frighten him to see military works in his county. I should have been rather afraid that my hon. friend would take umbrage at such a thing being done. I am glad he is coming back to the idea that we might establish that school in his county, and I congratulate him on his conversion. Now, there is no doubt that the place selected is a suitable place for such a military school. The school that we have had, that at St. Johns, is situated at some distance from Montreal. It has been, and is to-day, rendering great service. Still, it was certainly desirable that we should have a military school near Montreal. For some years the question has been discussed and military authorities have been considering the question. I am glad that my hon. friend (Sir Frederick Borden) has been able to select so good a site for this purpose. A number of sites were suggested to the government. The Minister of Militia has given his best consideration to these, and has come to the conclusion that the site on the other side of the river, at Montreal South, near Lon-gueuil, is the best available. There is a special reason which, I think, should commend it to the House, and that is the land already belongs to the government. It had been advertised for sale, if I remember well, some years ago, but we could not get the price we expected.
You can get $100,000 for it now.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
It is a very suitable site, and one easy of access to the people of Montreal, more so than almost any place that could be selected on the Island of Montreal. At one time, there was not much communication with Longueuil from the city of Montreal. But there is now constant communication by vehicles crossing the reconstructed Victoria bridge. And the property of the government is just opposite the ferry boat landing, the ferry giving a Mr. HUGHES.
15-minute service during the summer. There is also railway communication. I think that, in all respects, it is the most suitable place that could be chosen. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier says that the government will have to incur large expense in drainage works and other improvements. But if we were to purchase the property the hon. gentleman has in mind there would be the same expense.
Everything is there now.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Besides, it is not near the river as is the site which has been selected.
Has the government sold any part of its property in Montreal South?
Not since I have known anything about it. I think there are one or two schools situated on it that have been there for many years. But nothing has been sold of late, and nothing will be sold.
Has anything been sold in the last two years?
No.
Has the government purchased any other property in Montreal South?
No.

I think that covers all the items under vote No. 139. Perhaps we might take up No. 140 under which there are two or three military items for Ontario . that stood over.
Kingston Royal Military College, additional dormitory accommodation for cadets, $30,000.

Does any hon. gentleman desire information as to this item?
If not, it might be considered carried.
We should have more information from the Minister of Militia before this is carried.

I have a memorandum on the subject from the commandant of the college; but I have not it here, because I understood the reciprocity debate was coming on to-day, and so did not bring it. I am not prepared, therefore, to go on with this item; so it would be better to let it stand. I will be prepared, when it comes up again, to give all information.

Better let all the military items stand.
Public Works-Uhargeable to Income-Generally-Construction of immigration buildings, $15,000.

This is to construct buildings of a smaller class required to

meet the necessities of localities, which necessities arise very often without long warning. Hon. members can understand that, as the western country is filling up very rapidly, cases of this character arise.
How much was spent out of this vote last year?

We erected a building at Unity,. Saskatchewan, did some work in the Halifax detention hospital, constructed a building at North Portal, on the international boundary, put up small buildings at Wilkie, Battleford and Saskatoon, leaving unexpended of last year's vote $7,707.40.
Where may we expect this to be expended?
This is a general vote for experimental farms all over the Dominion.
I think the minister should give us a statement of the places where these expenditures will be made.

I could not do that, but I can say where the expenditures were made last year. We expended last year at Nappan, $343; Rossland, $39; Brandon, $864; Indian Head, $515; Lethbridge, $15; Agassiz, British Columbia, $780; Ottawa experimental farm, $11,251; additional office building, $7,517.
I asked the minister how he proposed to expend the amount we are now voting.
I cannot give the details, for the reason that it has been customary each year to take a vote for $25,000, and those expenditures are made upon the request of the Minister of Agriculture.
Perhaps the Minister of Agriculture could give us an explanation?

This item is larger than it was last year, because of the fact that the number of farms has increased. We have added to the number of farms by purchasing a new property, The first year while that property is being equipped 100}
it is paid for out of another vote, which appears in the estimates under the heading of Agriculture, Arts and Statistics. But when the farms are established, then any additional buildings or repairs that are required are paid for out of the vote in. the Public Works Department which is; now under discussion. I have not with me at the moment the details how it is expected to expend this amount of money in the next year, but I will be able to give them when the Agricultural estimates are down. The buildings at the Central Experimental farm here require considerable additions and repairs, which will have to be made. Some of the houses here have got into a bad condition, and must be attended to.
Does that mean that my hon. friend was neglecting his duty?

No, it means that we have been carrying them along as far as we reasonably could without making extensive repairs. But the time has been reached when an overhauling has to be done. We have expended a little from time to time. For instance, the house of the director at the Central Experimental farm will require next year a complete overhauling. Dr. Saunders has been careful not to expend anything that was not absolutely necessary, but something must now be done. This item applies, not only to the Central farm, but to all the branch farms. There was a time a few years ago , when this item was only $10,000 a year; last year it was $20,000, and now we ask for $25,000. I may mention another item of expenditure. Some years ago we undertook to lay down cement walks around the buildings of the Central farm, for the reason that such walks would last practically forever. Formerly we used to lay down wooden sidewalks, which had to be repaired frequently.
Is it customary, after an experimental farm has been established and equipped, to charge necessary repairs to the Department of Public Works?

We have a vote in the estimates under Arts, Agriculture and Statistics for additional branch farms that we may buy; we make the purchase of those farms out of that vote. Then as soon as the farm gets into working order, we cease to take the necessary expenses out of that vote, and this vote would apply to it as to the older farms.
How many farms have been established this year?

This last year we have only established one new farm at Scott, in the province of Saskatchewan. I hope

before winter is over to get one or two more. I have also purchased two farms in the province of Quebec within the last few months. One of these is completely equipped as it was purchased, the other will require considerable to be laid out upon it, but this vote will not be applicable to that. But as soon as the farms are purchased and the necessary buildings -are erected, then this vote would be applicable for repairs.
Does the minister get_ an estimate of the cost of the new buildings and improvements on buildings, or does he ask for a lump sum?
The sum is based upon the estimate of the farm staff as to what will be required in the ensuing year.
Then it is only what you *expect to need?
This is an estimate of what we want to provide for.
Can the minister tell us whether this vote includes any provision for a dairy building at Agassiz, or if that has been otherwise provided for?
The changes at Agassiz which my hon. friend refers to will be taken out of this vote.
Is it the intention to erect a dairy building there and pay some attention to dairying in connection with the Agassiz farm?
It. is intended to so rearrange and reorganize the buildings there as to establish a good dairy farm.

Before you take up the next sub-item, I would like to say that the other day the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Sharpe) asked whether any of the departments had purchased land from the Grand Trunk Pacific Development Company, and I told him that I was not aware of it, and said that nothing had been purchased by my department. In answer to a question, 'he told me that he had the Department of Agriculture in mind. My hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture being present, 1 would be very glad if he would be good enough to make a statement, so that it may go on ' Hansard ' for the information of the hon. gentleman.

A little over a year ago I entered into negotiations for the purchase of a piece of land near the station of Scott, *on "the Grand Trunk Pacific railway between Saskatoon and Edmonton. I am speaking now from memory, but I think there are 223 acres of land which I purchased from the Urand Trunk Pacific Development Company. This area was part of the land which Mr. FISHER.
the company had acquired from the government under the arrangement with them for town sites along their line. I secured it from them at exactly the same price as they paid to the government, plus the interest between the time that they purchased from the government and the time at which I purchased from them, so that it was practically just taking back the land which had been granted to them under the arrangement for town sites. The land is immediately adjacent to the town site of Scott. It comprises a quarter-section, and the portion of another quarter-section, which lies between that quarter-section and the railway track. The railway track is the northern boundary, the main road out of Scott to the south is the eastern boundary, and it. comprises, I think I am correct in saying, 223 acres, all of it absolutely virgin soil. None of it had been ploughed or touched until we did work on it last summer, and it is of the highest character and quality as prairie soil. I hope to be able to establish a station there, which will be of great value to the communities subservient to it. I am giving this explanation in answer to the question that was asked.
Fire escapes for Dominion public buildings, $5,000.

This is to meet the demands for fire escapes upon public buildings throughout the Dominion. Sometimes there is a demand from the people occupying the buildings that fire escapes should be placed upon them, and sometimes the local by-laws require it. We did not spend the whole amount last year; in fact, only $478, but the chief architect tells me that it is desirable to obtain a vote for this amount so as to make provision for fire escapes as they may be required.
Is there any public competition in the supplying of these?
Sometimes, when the work is considerable, but ordinarily the work on each building costs only $100, or $150, or $200.
What system of fire escapes does the minister adopt? There is a considerable number of these in vogue in Canada, and I presume that the minister has arrived at some decisions with regard to them.

They are all of iron, and they are all of the usual character. At Long.ueuil public building the work was done by the Capital Scale, Brass & Foundry Iron Company; they made the fire escape of iron and erected it at a cost of $195. At Clinton there was a balcony fire escape erected at a cost of $107, and at Cornwall there was a fire escape erected at a cost of $348. I have not the particulars of that, but it was the ordinary class of iron fire escape.

Public buildings, generally, $10,000.

This is to make provision for public buildings throughout the Dominion. It is an item which has been voted from year to year, and it is for demands that are made with respect to matters which are not otherwise provided for. Last year, up to the 27th of December, out of this vote there were paid the following amounts:-
