Leaving unexpended on the 28th December, 1910, a balance of $2,405.61. This is used for travelling expenses, stationery and printing, telegraphy and other miscellaneous items.
Would the minister explain what the stationery and printing are required for?

They are required for the chief architect's office and the clerk of works offices.
and the Imperial buildings and the government operates the elevators, whereas we occupy only a part of the Trafalgar building, and the owner runs the elevator.
I understood the minister to say that the foundation of the driveway was solid concrete. I have been told that it was gravel and crushed stone rolled. Which is it?
Solid concrete.
There is a new iron fence on the parliament grounds for which I cannot find an appropriation in the estimates.

I am glad to have an opportunity of explaining. The old fence upon Mackenzie avenue was no longer necessary, and we moved it together with the stone foundation to the parliament grounds ; using the services of our own men, and doing the job at comparatively little expense.
Heating, including salaries of engineers, firemen and watchmen, $133,000.
Have increases of salaries been given?

In quite a number of cases.
Tobacco curing, experimental stations, $5,000.

This is a revote. We obtained $5,000 last year, but it was not expended. The Department of Agriculture are again asking for it this year. The idea is to use it for the establishment of tobacco experimental stations.
ATe there any such stations now, and if so, where are they situated?

I might give my hon. friend the details of the expenditure in connection with this service made during the fiscal year 1909-10. At St. Cesaire, Quebec, there was erected a drying room, with two metallic ventilators, and a curing room, at a cost of $610. At St. Jacques de L'Achi-gan, Quebec, there was a curing barn erected, also a drying room and ventilators at a total expenditure of $586. At Colchester, Ontario, there was a curing barn erected, with a basement, two drying kilns, a Tack of two arches for heating, cement floors, excavation, costing $2,636 30. At Ottawa there was some work done at a cost of $310, all out of this vote.
Ottawa public buildings, elevator attendance, $26,000.
Do not the owners of the leased buildings provide the elevator attendance?
How are they given?1
We give such increasesr as we think are justifiable upon the report of the foremen of the heads of the department.
Have any been refused increases?
Yes. We try to reward merit, and give fair compensation for service rendered.
Who are judges of that?
We obtain reports from the chief architect and the foremen or superintendents, and the recommendation comes to the deputy minister and finally to the minister.
On what grounds were increases refused last vear? Can the minister give a list of the applications for increases made, the number granted, the number refused, and the grounds for refusal ?	_
I will get the information as far as possible, but of course, an application may be refused without the grounds being stated.
Last year the total amount paid for this service was $118,000, and this year you are asking $133,000.

It depends on the lease. Mr. PUGSLEY. That was for the year We occupy the whole of the Regal building ending 31st March, 1910, and the present

estimates are for the year ending 31st March, 1912, and there are additional men and increases of salaries which would account for the difference.
Was the $125,000 asked for last year expended?
It is anticipated that it will all be expended by March 31, next.
How does it come that there is this large increase of $8,000?
I can give the estimate. Coal is estimated to cost $62,655.
Is coal higher?
Anthracite coal $6.90, slack bituminous $4.70, cannel $8.75, and blacksmith $7.
You are paying higher prices?
Those are the prices of the lowest tenderer, Messrs. Heney & Son. Then there is the heating of the Canadian militia building and wages.
What additional buildings are you going to heat, and employ officials in, this year?

The Regal building, the Naval building, the new Museum, and the building which has been erected as a peat testing depot. Wages of the heating staff including coal men, wood men, &c., $46,556. Then there are contingencies which cover things for which it is impossible to provide with absolute certainty, $7,585, the total being $133,000 which it is assumed by the chief architect we will require for the year ending March 31, 1912.
Repairs, including ventilation and lighting, furniture, &c., $225,000.

An enormous amount is paid each year for new furniture for these buildings, and a large staff of men is employed under this item. I have been informed that about two-thirds of them do nothing at all, they simply draw their pay.
Would the hon. gentleman give the names of any in regard to whom he is so informed?
The .hon. gentleman is not sincere in saying that, it ii ridiculous.

I am perfectly sincere for this reason that if he has reliable information of any men on the staff of the department lying around not earning wages, I would have it looked into, and if the charge were substantiated have the men dismissed.
I do not believe the minister is sincere when he Says he would have them dismissed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am afraid the hon. member must not doubt the sincerity of the minister.
I forgive the hon. gentleman.
I do not want to break the rules of the House, but I wish to say what I think.
Urder.
The hon. gentleman will not give me the names anyway?

At all events there are several hundred men employed under this item, and, as I am informed, one-half or two-thirds of these men are simply there drawing their pay. The minister asks me to give their names. In the first place it would take up two or three pages of ' Hansard ' to give the names of all the men I believe are not employed. But in addition to that look at the enormous amounts paid out every year for furniture in this building. In the last five years over $1,000,000 have been paid out simply ior repairs and furniture, for the buildings here in Ottawa. Is this expenditure of about a quarter of a million dollars a year to continue forever, or is there likely to be a reduction of this vote?
The hon. gentleman will see that this vote is not entirely for furniture. It is for repairs for furniture and also for ventilation and lighting, and different items of that kind.
It does not include the supply of any electric current or gas?

No. The buildings are very large, they contain many "rooms which are all lighted and regarding which there must necessarily be a great deal of work to be done. There is necessarily a great deal of furniture requiring repairs, and new furniture must be bought from time to time. It would be impossible for me to go into all the details. That is a matter for the committee on public accounts. If my hon. friend wishes to inquire into any particular expenditure, he can have that inquired into in the Committee on Public Accounts, where the vouchers will be produced and the officials examined and the fullest information given. As regards the employees of the department, I cannot speak as to each individual, but I do know that we have a very reliable superintendent in whom my chief officers and myself have every confidence, and I would not believe, unless my hon. friend could vouch for it personally, that there are any number of men on the staff

who simply lie around and do not earn their wages. I can give the committee a statement of how this money will toe disposed of. To the clerk of the works staff for the men engaged under the clerk of works, $96,252.61; to the mechanical engineering staff, $38,688; for the purchase of lumber, paints, oil, glass, &c., and such ready-made furniture as cannot be constructed in the government workshop, $90,000, making a total of $225,000.. This also covers general repairs and maintenance in connection with gas, water, boilers, machinery, lavatories, &e.

I must disagree with the hon. minister when he says that the proper place in which to toring up this matter is the Public Accounts Committee. We all know that in that committee we can only bring up item by item, and the hon. minister knows that he, when he is there, and two or three of his assistants, do all they can to block investigations.

My hon. friend made that remark so often that he does not seem to realize its offensive nature. I have never observed, whenever I have been before the committee, any indication of any desire to block investigations. I am sure the hon. gentleman can have there every opportunity of investigating every one of these items if he so desires.
I am sure there are many members on both sides who will agree with me that facilities have not been given toy the minister and those associated with him to get at the bottom of facts.
My hon. friend must know' that I have only been myself in attendance on the committee at one of its sittings during this session. How, therefore, could I have assisted in blocking investigations?

There have only been one or two items in his department brought before that committee this session, which explains why the hon. minister was not there. I am speaking however, of past sessions. He knows quite well, that when we on this side were endeavouring to find out if there were not unnecessary expenditures in his department, there were always difficulties thrown in our vray. We asked for a special committee to investigate the department, as was given in the case of the Marine and Fisheries Department, but we were refused. If a similar committee were appointed, my own impression is, that it would show that the Public Works Department is in even a worse condition than was the Department of Marine and Fisheries. My hon. friend must know that there were good grounds for an investigation. He must have felt that in the case of certain expenditures in
his department, there was no doubt robbery and rascality.
Nobody observed that but the hon. gentleman himself. [DOT]

Men on both sides admit it, and the press as well. From the Atlantic to the Pacific the newspapers have been showing up these things in the Public Works Department. There was therefore, ample ground for an investigation into that department, but of course, that investigation was never given. If the hon. minister would agree to give such a commission as was appointed to investigate into the Marine and Fisheries Department, we could let all these items go through without discussion. Will he now, should we propose to have an investigation of that kind, consent to give it and thus save all these discussions on his estimates ?
accounts before the Public Accounts Committee, he would not for worlds have these vouchers presented
Why not?
Because he would have convincing evidence under oath that there could be no objection to these accounts, and that would cause him grave disappointment.

No one would be better pleased than I if it could be known that all the accounts in the Auditor General's Report represented payments honestly made in the public interest. But the minister knows that it is impossible for any person to judge whether these accounts are right or not. All we can do is to look over them, and if we see an item that looks suspicious bring it before the Public Accounts Committee. And the minister knows that seventy-five out of a hundred cases brought before the Public Accounts Committee have certainly looked very bad under investigation. He knows also that the facts discovered by the Public Accounts Committee would justify a general investigation into the department. Take this Bathurst dredging of which the minister was speaking. He knows that it was admitted in the Public Accounts Committee that through a mistake, $30,000 or $31,000 was spent that would not have been spent but for that mistake.
That all appeared before the Committee on Public Accounts.
I admit that. It was shown that a wrong
A wrong on the part of whom?
Some one in the Public Works Department.
No, it was a mistake on the part of the Great Northwestern Telegraph Company. If the hon. gentleman will call the manager of that company, that can be established.
There were other cases. For instance, the St. John dredging [DOT]-the Mayes matter. There was a commission paid there that went to the middleman wrongfully.

Not wrongfully.
Mr.,REID (Grenville). I am giving these items to show that we were justified, and are justified now, in asking a commission of investigation. There was the case of the saw-dust wharf where the middleman again appeared. The minister could not conscientiously state that that was a fair bargain in the interest of the country.
Absolutely.

Then I believe that the minister is the only man on either side of this House that believes it. Then, we have the Gaspereau dredging, where the minister had the report of his own engineer, stating 20c a fair price and gave it out at 90 cents a yard. These are just a few instances. Now, here is an expenditure of $225,000 a year. How are we going to investigate that before the Public! 'Accounts! Committee ? Why it would take the whole session. The first thing, some one will want to know-what I have been trying to find out-what becomes of the old furniture. We are constantly putting in new furniture ; what becomes of the old:
It is sold at public auction.
Is there a statement of that?
Certainly, a full statement.
That part of it may be all right. Then we hear reports of there being more men than are necessary.
My hon. friend must not believe all he hears.

But I believe what I hear repeated under oath in the Public Accounts Committee. If the minister would give us this investigation by Judge Cassels, or some man of that character, all this would be cleared up, and, if it were proved to be as the minister represents it, it would be to his credit and it would save a lot of discussion on these items. I, for one, do not believe that this large expenditure is necessary. It did not cost that much years ago, and it has been increasing year after year since this government came into power.

It would be the easiest thing in the world for my hon. friend, if he has any reason to suspect that the accounts included in this vote of $225,000 are not correct, that more men are employed than are needed, that higher wages are paid than ought to be paid, to call the proper officials before the Public Accounts Committee and learn the exact facts. The difficulty with my hon. friend is that he does not seem to wish to avail himself of the Public Accounts Committee to investigate these matters. He has referred to two or three cases whieh he gives as evidence of the great need of investigating thoroughly the Department of Public Works. He cites the dredging at Gaspereau, also what is known as the Mayes matter, and the dredging at Dalhousie. Is that all?
It would take me all the afternoon to give all the cases.
These are only samples.

When you consider that there has been an expenditure of from $12,000,000 to $15,000,000 a year by the Public Works Department, I think I ought to be well satisfied that the hon. gentleman, with all his industry, with all his digging and delving into the accounts, has only been able to call attention to three items.
I could easily give more.

When the hon. gentleman names these three off-hand, he, of course, gives the three that are of the most striking character. And what are they? Take the Mayes contract. It is said that a gentleman associated with him received a certain amount from the contractor, Mr. Mayes. In order that there should be any wrong-doing in connection with that which reflected on the department when it was presided over by the late minister

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The point of order has been raised of the relevancy of this discussion. The item before the committee is-
Repairs, including ventilation and lighting, furniture, &c., $225,000.
Any arguments used should be made to apply to that subject as closely as possibles

I think probably you are right. I was attempting to follow my hon. friend; however, I am content to let the matter rest as it is. It is desirable that we should all promptly obey your honour's ruling.
Telephone service, $19,000.
Last year I raised the question about the prices of telephones, because in some places we were paying much higher for them than in other places.

The hon. gentleman stated, if I remember rightly, that we were paying more for telephones in the government offices than private individuals were paying in the city of Ottawa; but I was able to show him that, taking all the services together, we paid less proportionately than was paid by the private citizens of Ottawa.

I notice, for instance, that we are paying $35 for a telephone in the office of the secretary of the Governor General, in the East block; we are paying $40 for the telephone of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, $40 per telephone in the House of Commons, $65 a year for the telephone in the office of the Speaker. Now, it strikes me that the government should have a regular annual rate for all telephones, the same as private citizens in the city of Ottawa. It may average
a lower price, as the minister says, but I do not understand why the charges should be made in this way. For instance, in this building, for the Speaker we pay $65, for the leader of the opposition, $55; messengers. $35; Committee on Agriculture, $40; distribution office, $40; sergeant at arms, $35, and so on. Then you go over to the Justice Department, and you pay $40.
How many telephones are there?
Altogether, 453. Desk phones, for instance, are subject to an extra charge.
It would be interesting to know how it comes that you have 453 telephones.

I can give the details. In the Department of Agriculture there are 18; Auditor General's office, 11; Census Department, 2; Customs Department, 11; Dominion police, 13; Exchequer Court, 2; Finance Department, 11; Governor General, 11; Geological Survey, 10; House of Commons, 20, including those for the opposition as well as for the government side; Indian Affairs, 8; Inland Revenue, 14; Interior Department, 56; Justice, 18; Labour Department, 6; Mounted Police, 4; Minister of Finance, 32; Militia and Defence, 46; Parliamentary Library, 3; Post Office Department. 16; Privy Council, 12; Public Works, 58; Railways and Canals, 23; Secretary of State, 15; Printing and Stationery, 16; Trade and Commerce, 9; Senate, 7. I have all the details here, but it would take me till midnight to read them.
58 for the Public Works Department; that seems to be a great number.

These telephones are used in all the chief branches of the Department of Public Works, including, for instance, the shipyard and the workshop.
Rideau Hall, including grounds, improvements, furniture and maintenance, $35,000.
Is the department thinking of erecting a new building for the Governor General in the place of the present Rideau Hall?

My hon. friend may remember that previously to my becoming minister there had been a proposition to put a new facade upon Rideau Hall, and to undertake considerable improvements, and a vote had been taken, I think, of $100,000 for that purpose. Tenders had been called for, and shortly after I became minister the tenders were opened, and I think the proposed cost reached the sum of nearly $300,000. I was of the opinion that, while extensive improvements are needed, and while Rideau Hall, as it is at

present, is not creditable to this country- I say that advisedly-it is not creditable to this great and wealthy country; yet I did not feel that we could justify an expenditure of $300,000 in making additions and improvements to the present building. I am not speaking now for the government, because the government have not considered this matter; I am merely giving my ow7n opinion. I think probably it would be better to sell the present property, which, at a reasonable estimate, if cut up into city building lots, would easily bring $700,000. That is the opinion which the Ottawa Improvement Commission have expressed to me, and they have made, at my request, an estimate which I think is moderate. I would erect a new government house upon some commanding site in the vicinity of Ottawa, and I would erect a building which would be a credit to this country, which would be fitting for the future Governors General who come here, and satisfactory to the people of this country for the next hundred years. However, this is only my own opinion. I mention it to the hon. gentleman as a partial answer to his question, and also as an explanation why we did not go on with the proposed improvement at Rideau Hall pursuant to the vote of parliament. As I have said, that amount seemed to me more than I would be justified in placing in the estimates under the circumstances.

I may frankly say that when I go down to Rideau Hall and look at the buildings, I think they are a disgrace to this country, and not befitting the high office of Governor General. But what I object to is that every year the government comes forward with large sums for repairs _ and improvements to Rideau Hall. I think the amount the minister is paying annually for repairs would pay the interest on the cost of a fine new residence such as he mentions.
This money is not all being expended on the building; it is also for renewals, repairs to furniture, &c.

It may be this year, but I think the minister will agree with me that there have been in the past and probably will be in the future amounts expended on that building for repairs. Instead of repairing that old building I think it is time for the minister to consider the question of providing new quarters and getting rid of these premises, probably in the way he says. If he can get $700,000 out of that property I cannot see why he should have to ask parliament for any appropriation to provide a new building. Does the minister think that amount would not be sufficient to erect a new building on another site?
Mr. PUGSLEY

It ought to give a very fine building.
Dominion buildings, furniture, $15,000.
Has it been definitely decided to erect a new building on Sussex street?
Yes, that is the definite decision.

I think it is a serious mistake for the government of this country to erect a magnificent building back on Sussex street. You have already started building on the park by erecting a hotel there, which, I think, was a great mistake, but now that it is there, I would suggest that it is only proper that this new block be built along the face of the park right from the hotel, and facing west. I think then we would get the benefit of the building, and as you have already purchased the property on Sussex street, you could do away with Mackenzie avenue, and continue the park out to Sussex street. You would then have a magnificent park with the 'buildings now there removed, the new building would be seen by everybody if it were placed along the face of the park. This would be a very great improvement upon the present policy of the department. I think it would be a serious mistake to spend $1,000,000 or $2,000,000 in erecting a great building back on Sussex street, and I hope the department will never agree to a policy of that kind. I believe they could erect this building along the face of the hill and it would be a very great improvement on what they contemplate doing, and it certainly would be a magnificent site for offices. Then we would have the parliament buildings all within view of the bridge. As you have started to build on that park I do not see why you should not continue as I suggest it would be very much better than what you propose.

My hon. friend is the last contributor to the new ideas as to the proper location for the departmental buildings. I have had a great many suggestions, but I have felt that as parliament, before I became minister, made an appropriation for the payment for the ground between Mackenzie avenue and Sussex street, and as a very extensive area of land has been bought, it was my duty to go ahead and provide for the construction of the building upon this ground. 1 might suggest other places in the city which, in the judgment of some people, perhaps in the judgment of myself, might possess advantages which that site does not present, but that is the site which has been approved of, it is the site which has been bought and paid for, and it is now owned by the government. Perhaps it is inaccurate for my

hon. friend to say that the buildings are to be erected on Sussex street. They "are also to have a frontage upon Mackenzie avenue, and upon this park, and run through to Sussex street so that there will be a frontage on both streets. I am afraid I cannot hold out any hope to my hon. friend that the site will be changed. The present plan is to go ahead, and build upon the site which we have bought and paid for.

I can only say that I think.it is a serious mistake on the part of the government.
Dominion buildings, lighting, $140,000.
This is an increase of $5,000 owing to the increase in the number of buildings.

I suppose that under the head of lighting one might refer to the electric wiring of this building, and particularly to that in the library. I am not sufficiently skilled to say whether it is defective or whether there is any danger of fire from it. It appears that in certain places at least it has a very exposed look, and we know that a few days ago there was a fire in the corridor leading to the library. It occurred during a time when there was a number of people about to see that it was extinguished. I do not know whether it was due to any defect in the wiring of the building, but it is a matter worthy of consideration. Perhaps the minister could assure the committee that in the condition of the wiring there is no risk to the valuable collection of books in the-library.

The chief architect tells me that h'is attention was called to an incipient fire which might be regarded more as smoke than blaze and the best judgment he has been able to form is that probably there has been a little waste paper and somebody has thrown a match down while lighting his pipe or cigar. He does not think that it came from any defect in the electrical wiring. However, the suggestion is one that is worthy of careful attention. It is of importance that the wiring should receive careful attention. We have an expert staff whose duty it is to look after these matters, and I shall see that the hon. gentleman's remarks are brought to their notice so that if there is anything that requires attention it will be looked into.
The minister had a fire in his own office. Was noi that from electric wires crossing one another or something of that kind?
I thought it was.

Well there must have been some looseness about the wiring in that case.
Mi*. PUGSLEY. Yes, there is a danger always.

I think there is more danger of spontaneous combustion than from defective electric wiring. I was downstairs at the long distance telephone when an hon. gentleman who sits close to the minister asked me to look into the room which is just beyond the long distance telephone. I looked in, and I am sure that if there is not spontaneous combustion in the building pretty soon it will be a miracle. This gentleman told me that the same condition is to be found all over the building.
What room is that?
Just back of the telephone.
I suppose there was a lot of waste material in it?

It was not fit for a pig pen. That is the care that is taken of the building, and yet my hon. friend says that there are experts looking after it. All he has to do is to appeal for confirmation to an hon. gentleman who sits near him, and who knows the condition to which I refer because he spoke to me himself about it. The care which is taken of this building is the same as that which is taken of the grounds.

If there be any fault it would be with the -staff of the House of Commons, and not with the staff of the ' Public Works Department. I will have the matter brought to the notice of the super intendent of the House of Commons building.

I am not an electric light expert, but I can see that wires are strung in the various rooms of this building in a haphazard manner and not in accordance with the requirements of the underwriters. Of course, this building was erected years ago when fireproof construction -had not reached its .present development, and I believe it worthy of the attention of the minister to see that an electric wiring expert should go carefully over all the wiring in the building.

We have an electric expert constantly engaged in that work. So long as the wires are properly insulated there is no danger, but nevertheless the remarks of my hon. friend will be noted by the chief architect, and if possible, greater precaution will be taken.
In room 68 there are from 10 to 15 electric lights hanging by long cords which .are all intertwined, and it would seem to me to be dangerous.

I have been told by those who seem to know that the wiring

of the building at present is not up to the underwriters requirements.
We do not insure our buildings, and therefore, the underwriters' experts do not examine them. The chief architect tells me that the electrician reports it is up to the standard of the underwriters.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: To my knowledge there is wiring in the new wing that will not pass the underwriters' inspection.

In the Public Accounts Committee last year the hon. member for North Ontario discovered, notwithstanding all the obstacles that were thrown in his way, that $5,000 or $6,000 of the money of the people was wrongfully paid for electric lighting of the Woods and the Canadian buildings. When this discovery was made we were promised that not only would the contract be cancelled, but that suit would be entered against the Imperial Realty Company to make them refund to the public treasury the overcharges they made. Has that money been refunded?

Two years before I became minister the agreement was entered into, and I understand that then the chief architect thought it was better to pay by the meter so that the department would be charged for the electrical energy actually used. I believe that for a while the meter would be less than the flat rate. On principle I am entirely opposed to a flat rate but so long as there is a flat rate and a meter rate I suppose it is the duty of the department to get the cheaper rate. In the case of a public utility such as electric lighting-and I wish to say this publicly for the information of the city of Ottawa and the electric lighting company-it is in my judgment a gross injustice that the ordinary householder should be obliged to pay a meter rate which is higher than the flat rate which a large consumer of electricity such as the government can get. I believe there should be one rate, and one rate only in the case of public utilities of that kind just the same as in the case of the railways, which cannot give a cheap rate to the large dealer.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The railways make a carload rate.

Yes, but they must give the same rate for ten carloads as for one. However, that may be, when I became minister there was rendered to my department by the Imperial Realty Company, bills upon a meter basis and those bills were accompanied by bills, on their regular account forms rendered by the electric light department of the city of Ottawa, presided over by the city treasurer, Mr. Ellis, showing the indebtedness of the Imperial Realty Company or James W. Woods as the case Mr. JAMESON.
might be, to the city, for the amount of current consumed, based upon the meter rate. These bills were marked ' settled ' by the electric department of the city ; they were receipted as vouchers and they accompanied the bills which the Imperial Realty Company rendered to my department. Thus the city of Ottawa furnished those bills as being the vouchers based upon the meter rate of the amounts which the Imperial Realty Company asked my department to pay. After I became minister, the deputy minister was changed, the present deputy minister became the principal official of the department. If it had come to my notice or to the notice of the principal officers of my department that we were being charged by the Imperial Realty Company not the identical amounts which the Imperial Realty Company was paying to the electrical department of the city of Ottawa-
What would be the object in making out the cheques to the Imperial Realty Company, why not direct to the city of Ottawa?

I do not know.
Mr. SHARPE (Ontario! Would not that arouse suspicion?
No, because I would never dream that the treasurer of the city of Ottawa would issue a false voucher.

It is only fair to the city treasurer to state that the president of the Imperial Realty Company went to him and personally asked him to furnish the amount of electricity that was consumed on a meter basis. He said he did not know what purpose it was to be used for, he had been personally requested by the president of the company to furnish the amount on a meter basis. He did not get paid for it, and did not do it with intent to deceive the department.
So also the Imperial Realty Company say they did not do it to deceive the department.
But they did deceive the department.

But the fact is that Mr. Ellis, the treasurer of Ottawa, furnished these vouchers not simply as the amount consumed, on a meter basis, but as accounts showing the indebtedness of the Imperial Realty Company to the city of Ottawa for these amounts.
On an ordinary form.

On the account forms they always send out showing the indebtedness of the Imperial Realty Company to the city of Ottawa for the electric current consumed at the meter rate and upon a

meter basis. It may be true, as my hon. friend says, that the treasurer of Ottawa did not intend that this should be used to deceive the department.
He says he did not.

I am bound to believe him. I would be sorry to suspect people of dishonesty in face of their statements and without knowledge to the contrary, but the Imperial Realty Company say the same thing, that they did not intend to deceive the department. As a matter of fact they got the money and got it upon vouchers signed by the city of Ottawa upon the quantity of electric current consumed and charged upon the meter rate. And this is the important thing, that ever since I became minister and ever since the present deputy became deputy minister, these vouchers were rendered, and my department paid to the Imperial Realty Company the identical amount of these vouchers rendered by the electrical department of the city to the Imperial Realty Company as proofs to show that that was being paid to the city of Ottawa, the whole charge being based upon a meter rate. When the matter came on for investigation, as my hon. friend says, before the Committee on Public Accounts, evidently my hon. friend from North Ontario was furnished, and I am glad he was furnished, with the information which the proper officials of the city of Ottawa had withheld from my department.
It was not until I saw the suspicious looking documents in your file.

The hon. gentleman had access to all the files, we glady furnished them. When towards the latter part of the investigation it came to my knowledge that there was a difference between what these vouchers showed and what it was alleged had actually been paid to the city, and that these vouchers had been rendered to my department from time to time as being evidence of what the Imperial Realty Company was paying to the city, I asked the deputy minister to inform the committee that I would proceed to cancel the contract and to recover whatever amount had been paid by the department to the Imperial Realty Company in excess of what the Imperial Realty Company had paid to the city. In due course, after parliament rose, I had a request made to the city of Ottawa to furnish a statement of what amounts had actually been paid by the Imperial Realty Company.	That statement was not
furnished.	I then directed the deputy
minister to hand the matter over to the Department of Justice to look into the
whole question, and if the department was of opinion that there was a cause of action against the Imperial Realty Company, either individually or jointly with the city of Ottawa, to take proceedings for the purpose of recovering the difference.
Have you had a report yet?

No report has come to my knowledge as to what action has been taken by the Justice Department, but I understood some time ago that they had been requested to allow the matter to stand until counsel for the Imperial Realty Company, then absent, returned to Ottawa. I have not recently heard what further action has been taken by the Department of Justice.
The minister was going to lay on the table the two letters that constituted a contract between the Imperial Realty Company and the government.
I will see that they are brought here.

We would like to see them so as to form our own opinion as to the liability of the Imperial Realty Company. Speaking of the electric light and these accounts, the minister attempts to shift the responsibility on the shoulders of the city treasurer. In my humble opinion the Minister of Public Works or his department is a party to any fraud that has been committed.
I have not said there was any fraud, I did not use the word fraud.
That was the inference from your remarks.
My hon. friend as a lawyer knows that-there may be such a thing as a legal fraud which would give the right to recover money without actual intentional fraud.

The mere fact that these alleged statements were rendered by the city to the Imperial Realty Company and be the Imperial Realty Company to the government would alone excite suspicion in any person's mind. Why the necessity of keeping two sets of books and why pay the cheques to the Imperial Realty Company and have them transfer them over to the city of Ottawa? A person viewing that transaction would at once have his suspicions excited that there was something radically wrong, that a middleman must be getting a rake-off somewhere, and consequently if any one in the department had the slightest conception of the method of conducting business properly

and economically he would have investigated the matter. Why were not the cheques made payable direct to the city of Ottawa? If there was' any fraud or wrong committed on the department the department itself is partly guilty. What is the cost of lighting all the public buildings here in Ottawa?

There are in the public buildings lamps to which the current is supplied by the Ottawa Electric Company to the number of 15,929. Under the contract, the first 3,000 are charged at the rate of $2.25 per annum, making $6,750.
That is yearly.

It was originally a 10 years' contract. It has now expired, and has not yet been renewed. Then there are 12,929 lamps at $2, making $25,858. That is in addition to the lighting in the buildings, owned by the Imperial Realty Company. We have made a change through having cancelled the contracts under which we pay to the city a flat rate of $2 per lamp, that is for the Canadian building and the Railway Commission building. That includes all the electric lighting.
Is there any meter basis or is it all flat rates ?
All on a flat basis.
Is the contract let by tender ?
No.
Does the minister not think that since the city has a municipal plant as well as the Ottawa Electric Light Company, we might. get a more advantageous rate by inviting competition ?

There are just two rates in Ottawa, one flat and the other meter, and the two plants charge the same rates. When we made this change from meter to flat rate, we asked the city for the lowest rate and they gave it at $2.
The government contract is worth nearly half a million dollars. If they let that >by tender, could they not get a more advantageous rate ? Is it the intention to renew the contract for ten years ?
We are continuing under the expired contract at present. There are some questions pending for consideration which will have to be decided before we renew the contract.
Is it the intention to ask for tenders before renewing the contract ?

No. There are two rates, a flat rate and a meter rate. I do not think it would be right for my department to go to these companies and say: True, you have your flat rate and your meter rate, but this government is too poor or too mean to pay the same rate that other people pay, and we want you to reduce it. I would not be a party to doing that.
That objection might hold to any contracts the government might make.

Not at all. This is a public utility.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SASKATOON AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to oppose the second reading of this Bill, but I should like it to receive its second reading only upon the understanding that before passing this House the spelling of the word * Hudson ' would be changed to * Hudson's.' I do not want to take up the time of the House talking about trifles, but I cannot understand -what object there is, especially in an official proceeding such as the passing of a Bill through this House, in changing the good old, well-established spelling of the name Hudson's Bay. It is nearly fifty years ago since I was taught, as a schoolboy, that our word Hudson's Bay was always spelled with the ' s,' whereas the United States

river Hudson was spelled without the ' s '. I think that is a very good reason, if no ether existed, why we should adhere to the English method of spelling this word. It is a different word, and, however much we may admire modern improvements in spelling, we cannot change the name of the great company which had its charter now nearly 250 years ago, and which has made famous the world over the name Hudson's Bay. I think the very circumstance that we have our own expression, while the United States have theirs, that it is the English language we speak, and, therefore, that _we ought to look to England for our standards of orthography and geography, affords in itself reason enough why, in an official proceeding of this character, we ought to adhere to the expression Hudson's Bay, whatever newspapers and whatever other peojde may do about it.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.

Before going on with these items, I observe that my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) is spending a great deal of time on the estimates of his department The Minister of Public Works, we know, is a very hard-working man; he is active, he gets his estimates down here, he attends to them every night, and endeavours to get them through. There are other ministers of the Crown who are in charge of departments fust as important as the Department of Public Works. I am sure that the House would be very much pleased to see the estimates of some of the other ministers brought down here and discussed openly and freely, and it would be largely to the benefit Of the country if such were the case. For instance, I think we should have a few nights on the estimates of the department of the Minister of Finance, so as to relieve the burden from the Minister of Public Works. Then there is also the hon. gentleman (Sir Frederick Borden) in charge of the Department of Militia and Defence, and I know that the House is desirous of discussing his estimates for three or four nights. We never have the pleasure of having him with us at all, and I am sure I am voicing the sentiments of members on this side of the House when I say that the estimates of some other department should be taken up as well as those of the Department of Public Works. The estimates of the Public Works Department pall on the taste, and I think it would be well, the next- night when estimates are taken up, if we had, say, the Department of Militia and Defence under fire. Then, again, as I 101
have said before, we would like the estimates of the department of the Minister of Finance, and we should have a few nights with the Department of Agriculture, which deals with the largest interest and industry of the country. We like to discuss these items with the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Air. Fisher), as he is always willing to discuss them ad libitum and to give us a great deal of information. I feel convinced that the country is yearning and panting to hear from the Minister of Agriculture, and there are a great many members in the House on this side who are interested in farming matters, and who would like to have the estimates of the Department of Agriculture under review for some time. I cannot hope that the government will bring forward any estimates except those which they please, but 1 am sorry that they are placing the Minister of Public Works in the limelight every night and putting him to the front, so that we may smash him and do all kinds of things to him, when the other ministers ought to carry their end of the log just the same as he is carrying it. I hope that we may have a chance of discussing estimates other than those of the Department of Public Works.
Ottawa public buildings, lighting, $140,000.

When the committee rose at six o'clock the hon. the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) had made a very carefully worded statement in which he endeavoured to place the responsibility for the rake-off that had been made by the Imperial Realty Company on the city of Ottawa and the Imperial Realty Company rather than on the Department of Public Works. If that statement, as made by the minister, were borne out by the evidence in the Public Accounts Committee I do not think there would be any doubt in the minds of members of this House that both the city of Ottawa and the Imperial Realty Company were in collusion to defraud this government out of a large sum of money and as such should be prosecuted. Indeed, when the minister said he had placed the matter in the Justice Department he left the inference that such was his idea. While not attempting to defend the Imperial Realty Company I must say that my conception of the evidence before the committee was that the responsibility rested solely with the Public Works Department and not with them. The evidence showed -although we could not get the correspondence bearing on it-that there evidently had been a contract of some kind by which the Imperial Realty Company was to furnish the light to these particular buildings at a fixed rate, based on the rate paid by other consumers in the city. They were justly entitled to get whatever rate, they could from the original supplier o4 the power, and in the result they got *



much cheaper rate than they charged the government and they had a rake-off of a very large sum of money. If it is the belief of the minister that there was wrongdoing then he should have taken more active steps than to merely place the matter in the hands of the Justice Department, where it rests. We had a very similar transaction where the department installed an elevator in one of the public buildings when the lease stipulated that it should be installed by the proprietor of the building, and that case we were also told had been sent to the Department of Justice. We have to-night seen the Minister of Public Works with a remarkably tender conscience and with a remarkable idea of fair play and justice, holding up his hands in holy horror at the thought of asking a rich corporation to send in a tender for the supply of electric power. He told us that he would not for one moment be mean enough-I think that was the word he used-to ask for tenders for supplying all the power necessary for lighting all the public buildings and running the elevators in these buildings.

My hon. friend misunderstood me. What I said was that the companies had two rates: a meter rate and flat rate, and I did not think I would be justified in asking them to reduce the rate so as to bring it below what was charged to other people.

We are therefore to understand that the Minister of Public Works, having full charge of the people's money would not endeavour by asking for tenders, to get the best possible price for a service which costs a very large sum annually. The minister is very solicitous about an electric light company, the stock of which is selling at $163, or 63 over par, and which is paying very large dividends, to its shareholders. The minister in his tender solicitude for this company refuses! even to ask for tenders as an ordinary business transaction. I happen to have some knowledge of how this matter is dealt with in my part of the country where they develop a large amount of electricitv and sell the power to mining companies and others. The power companies sell at both -flat and meter rates, and yet there is not a single one of these large power consuming companies in the whole of my province which is paying the ordinary flat or meter rate. They all buy it at a fixed rate per horse-power per annum and they get their supply by tender at the lowest price. There is absolutely no reason as an ordinary business transaction why the Minister of Public Works should not follow the every day business custom and endeavour to buy the power which the government requires for these services at the lowest possible rate. There is absolutely no reason why tenders Mr. GOODEVE.
should not be asked for. It is very remarkable that the minister should all at once display such an extremely tender conscience lest he should offend these people by asking them to tender for power supply at a reasonable' rate to a large consumer like the government.

I have no tender feeling towards the company or the electrical department of. the city. I would be quite willing to get from them the lowest possible rate that can be obtained, but what I said was that I did not think it right that the government should take advantage of its position to try and get a lower rate than other customers in the city have to pay. Some get a meter rate and some a flat rate, and if we ask for a flat rate, or a meter rate we are entitled to get the same rate as other large consumers of electricity. But we have no right as a government to get our electricity, whether by flat rate or meter rate, at one cent less than the ordinary consumer pays. My regard is for the consumers and every dollar which the government may take out of the companies is so much money charged against the ordinary consumer. There should, in my judgment be the same rate to the poor man as to the rich, to the private individual as to the government. That would be the ideal system, but if there is to be a flat rate and a meter rate then I believe these rates should be under the control of the Bailway Commission and the government should not get a lower rate than any other consumer of electricity.
How many companies can supply power?
Two, the electrical department of the city and the Ottawa Electric Company.
Did the minister ask prices from both?

Did the Minister ask the price at which these two companies would supply the current?

They were conferred
with.
Public competition?
No.
Whv not?

Simply because there are only the two companies and we asked

them for the best rate they could give and we got it. We have done exactly what I would do if I owned a large building in the city that required lighting. They should have one price for all, whether a meter or a fiat rate price.

Does the minister mean seriously to tell me that if this company was asked to give a special wholesale rate for a large consumer it would -affect in the slightest degree the rate that they make to the ordinary consumer? In this very transaction we find that the Imperial Realty Company, whilst charging the government the regular meter rate, was getting a very much lower rate so that they had a rake-off of $3,000 or $4,000 a year on this building alone. Surely he does not expect this House to believe that the mere asking for a tender for a large supply of power at a low rate would affect the rate charged the ordinary customer. I am amazed that the minister should advance such an absurd argument.

In this case it is alleged that the Imperial Realty Company had a flat rate, and that the bills which were rendered by the city to the Realty Company and again by the Realty Company to the government were based upon a meter rate. I do not understand that there are two flat rates or two meter rates, but that there are two rates, one a meter and one a flat. If this company, as I think it should be, is subject to the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners or the board of the province of Ontario, which I think has also jurisdiction over electrical matters, the board would allow the company a fair and reasonable profit upon its investments, and therefore, the cheaper the rate at which the government could get its electricity the higher the rate which would have to be charged the ordinary consumer in order to enable the company to make a reasonable and fair profit. The government ought not to be able to get and ought not to seek to get electric lighting or gas lighting, whether by flat rate or by meter rate, at a lower cost than the ordinary consumer pays, whether by flat rate or by meter. That is my position and that is why I have not called for tenders, but have asked the electric company and the city to give us the lowest flat rate.
Were they both the same?
Yes.
Then why was the selection made.	.

The Ottawa Electric Company is supplying this building with light. The city already had their wires in the other building, and we thought as they were giving as low a rate as the Ottawa company we ought to continue with them.

The hon. member for Kootenay (Mr. Goodeve) must not be surprised at the position taken by the minister because his policy and that of his government is entirely in opposition to public tenders. Therefore, we must expect that when my hon. friend is dealing with a matter of this kind he will not ask for public competition. We tested the House upon that question, and my hon. friend the minister is on record. I have a motion here which was moved and voted on in the House:
That all the supplies purchased for the use of the various departments of the government should be procured on the basis of public tender and contract, under the direction of a competent purchasing commission, and with regard primarily to quality and price.
I suppose supplies would mean electrical current the same as other purchases. That is the policy the opposition laid down on the floor of the House on many occasions. The minister voted against this motion, and having voted against a policy of public competition he is very fearful lest two companies in the city of Ottawa might, get in competition with one another and; forsooth the government might get a cheaper price than some poor individual ins the city. Did any one ever hear of such a policy? Why does not my hon. friend be-frank in dealing with a matter of this kind, and put the transaction beyond suspicion by asking these two companies to give tenders? He had a splendid opportunity to. have public competition, he had one company competing with another in the capital city right at his hand, yet he ' says:	Oh, no, we must not do that, we
might get something cheaper than we ought to. That part of it is a brand new doctrine; the other part is an old story, the policy of the hon. gentleman and his government is in opposition to public competition, and here is a splendid exemplification of the policy; indeed it will point out to the country the difference between the policy of this government and of the opposition. My hon. friend need not be at alt concerned about the citizens of Ottawa.

I venture to say that during all the years the Conservative party was in power they never asked for tenders for electric lighting, and my hon. friend cannot find a single case in any part of the Dominion where they called for tenders for lighting by electricity or gas. They took it for granted that the ordinary charge to the public was the fair and reasonable charge to pay, and he cannot say we are paying one cent more than the large consumers in Ottawa are paying.

When my hon. friend's party were in opposition they constantly condemned the Conservative government, because we did not ask for public competi-

tion, that was one of the chief planks in the platform of the party.

Not in electricity and gas. I think I am safe in saying that in 1896 the government owned the plant. When my hon. friend asked why, when there are two plants in this city, we did not invite competition, the only excuse he has to offer is that if he did, the department might possibly have got its_ lighting done cheaper than some individuals would. Might I ask him if he proposes to continue that kind of policy.

This is no new policy of the Department of Public Works, because when discussing an item regarding the museum in the city, the minister said that the contractor had tendered too low and that the departments, in order to make up the loss, gave him extras without calling for tenders, and that contractor is still going on supplying extras on that building from year to year. With regard to the particular item under discussion, the Realty Company had a meter rate with the electric light company while charging the government a flat rate, and were making a large profit. It would appear to me, that a company, in fixing a flat rate, would base it on the maximum quantity of light that could be used and would consequently, charge more than if they charged only for the actual light consumed. If for no other reason, it would be advisable for the government to see if they could not get tenders to supply the light by ampere or horsepower for government purposes.

It is very difl&cult to satisfy hon. gentlemen opposite. We have been condemned because we did not get a flat rate and now we are being condemned because we did insist on a flat rate. In reply to the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain), I may say that, as at present advised, I shall continue to do what we have done, namely, find out what is the best flat rate and then give the contract to the company which charges the cheapest. In this particular case, both companies have the same flat rate, and so we divided the contract between them.
The two companies will know just how to handle the hon. minister in the future.
Just as they know how to handle all other consumers of electricity.
What has become of our own electric apparatus which we had for manufacturing light in the building here ? It gave us good light, and gave it to us cheap.
The chief architect tells me that was in operation about 20 years ago, and was done away with when the Conservatives were in office.

Before recess, I asked the minister about .the contract for the Woods building and the Canadian building, and he answered everything I did not ask him about. He talked about flat rates and meter rates. I remember that when the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe), was trying to find out what the Realty Company paid the city of Ottawa for lights in order to compare that with the very high price they were charging this government, the minister and everybody else in his department did everything possible to prevent our getting that information.

I deny that most positively. That question came up some time ago, and the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe), said I was in the committee room when objection was taken to the production of the written contracts between the city and the Imperial Realty Company. I replied that I was not at that meeting. Through the kindness of the hon. member for Kootenay (Mr. Goodeve), I was enabled to see the appendix 3 of the proceedings of that committee, and in looking over the proceedings of the 22nd of April, -that being the day when that contract was asked for, and the Chairman ruled it out-I find I was not present. At a later meeting of the committee an attempt was made by the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe), to give hearsay evidence of that contract which had been ruled out, and I objected. Any law student of a month's standing will say that I was absolutely correct.

I was present, and I have pretty good eyesight, and I am prepared to state that the minister was present. But that has nothing to do with the argument. Whether he was present or not, he is responsible for the Public Works Department, and the department did everything they could to prevent the Public Accounts Committee from getting any idea what the Realty Company were paying the city of Ottawa for the light they are furnishing this government. But the department, instead of acting in the public interest, and giving us an opportunity of ascertaining what we were paying in overcharge for light, did everything they could to prevent us from getting the information. We all remember that after it had been fully discussed in the House, the Deputy Minister of Public Works came into the committee the next morning and went on the stand, and the first thing he said was : We have decided, not only to cancel the

contract, but to bring an action against the Realty Company to compel them to return the money. Now, the Minister of Public Works stated just before recess that no doubt they had paid more than they ought to have paid ; but he said there was a document furnished by the treasurer of the city of Ottawa which was handed him by the secretary of the Realty Company regarding the price of light ; they discovered that this document was a false document, and yet it was upon this document that the Department of Public Works issued their cheque. Consequently somebody was obtaining money under false pretenses. Then the Minister of Public Works tells us that he has handed that matter over to the Justice Department. I say it was the duty of the Public Works Department to take up this question themselves and find out who is to blame, and compel a return of the money to the public coffers. He says now he has turned it over to the Justice Department, and he really doesn't know whether they are going to do anything or not. The department has paid over this money on the strength of a false document ; I do not care whether it was issued by the treasurer of the city of Ottawa, or at the instance of the secretary of the Realty Company ; the fact is that the cheque was issued on the strength of that false document. It is not flattering to the Public Works Department that they should have issued a cheque on a false document. Now, I want to know from the Minister of Public Works whether they intend to go after the Realty Company, or the city treasurer of Ottawa, I do not care which, whichever one is guilty of making this false document. I want the minister , to tell us whether any effort is toeing made to punish those who were guilty, as shown by that investigation. We were never able to discover in the Public Accounts Committee what price the Realty Company were paying the Ottawa Electric Light Company for the light they were furnishing to the government. I say that the Public Accounts Committee is not a place where the government should stand on fine legal points, when we are endeavouring to get at facts vital to the public interest. There should toe no objections raised in the Public Accounts Committee, particularly by a minister of the Crown, whose duty it is to guard the public interest. But our experience has been that, no matter what minister is before the committee, he acts as if he had received a large retainer in order to protect the witness who is there for the purpose of giving information. I want to know where this is going to end. I want to know whether the minister is going toi continue the farce, or whether he intends to take any steps to force these parties to return the money.

I only repeat to my hon. friend that the papers in the case have been handed over to the Justice Department, with the request that they will look into the case, and take such action as they may think proper to take. The Justice Department is the proper tribunal to which -to send cases of this kind.

I think the minister is in error when he stated that the Conservatives were in power twenty years ago when this change was made about the electric lighting. I was here twenty years ago, and my hon. friend was not ; and I know that at that time the government generated the light in this building, and then the plant was moved down below the hill on the edge of the river. The power was at work when the change of government took place, and it was the late Mr. Tarte who* made the change, and put in these lights, we have now. Those are the facts, and the minister was trying to mislead the House when he stated that the change was mad * twenty years ago.

The information I gave was furnished to me by the chief architect, I could have no personal knowledge of the matter myself.

The Minister of Public Works has taken the ground that large users of public utilities should be placed upon the same footing and pay the same prices as the smaller ones, and that the government should be placed upon the same.footing as a private individual. Now I do not think the great majority of business people in this country would consent to that proposition, but whether it is sound or not, I would like to commend the Minister of Public Works to the Minister of Railways, who, during the deliverance of his budget speech on the Intercolonial railway last year, and the year before, complained to the House that the government was compelled to purchase its supplies for the Intercolonial at the same price as everybody else, although it was a large purchaser of supplies, and if it were not compelled to publish the price at which they were purchased in the Auditor General's Report, they would be able to obtain goods at a lower rate than the general public. He advanced the argument that the accounts of the Intercolonial railway should not be published in that report, because the company would then be able to purchase its supplies cheaper. Only three days ago, in this House, the hon. member for Argenteuil (Mr. Perley) brought up the case of an excursion train being taken from Levis to Montreal and return, a distance of some 326 miles, and that tickets were sold on that train for $1.50 each, or less than one-half cent a mile return, whereas the rate confirmed by the Railway Commission, and the minimum rate to be charged by other lines of railway was $2.70 for the same service. There was a case of a public utility, but the Minister of Railways justified the smaller charge on the ground that he was serving a larger number, that a larger number of tickets was sold, and that the government was making money out of the transaction. So on these two points the Minister of Railways is diametrically opposed to the Minister of Public Works.

The statement made by the Minister of Railways was an extraordinary one. He said it was not his place to try to beat any one down, or get them to lower their figures under what they were charging others in a contract like this. The principle has been recognized by this government that it is their duty not to expend public moneys, where the expenditure exceeds a certain sum, without asking Mr. PUGSLEY.
for tenders. Both sides of the House have put themselves on record in a resolution to that effect. Therefore it is not for the Minister of Public Works to say, I am not going to ask this company or any other company to furnish us with light at a lower rate than they are furnishing it to other customers. His duty is to ask for tenders, and if the company is prepared to tender at a lower rate than they are selling to others, on account of the larger contract, then it is for that company to say what they will tender for, and if they tender to serve the government lower than other parties, it is the duty of the minister to accept that tender.

I would ask the Minister of Public Works to furnish the House with the date when the late Mr. Tarte made the change, and installed, the lights we have now. I would also like him to say what was done with the plant the government then owned. Was it handed over to the parties who are now furnishing the light? We had a good plant and wiring, what became of them?
I will get the details for my hon. friend.

In 1896 when this government came into power these buildings were lighted with gas. At that time the government were paying more for gas than they should, as the price of gas has gone down since. At that time the cost of lighting all the public buildings in the city of Ottawa, according to the Auditor General's Report, was $23,483, in 1896, when the Conservative party went out of power. At the present time, under the Liberal party, it is costing this country $53,000 per year to do exactly the same service as was done in 1896. In addition to that we have now electric power, should we not get that electric power much cheaper than gas?
That has not been my experience.
Then the minister must have been dealing an awful lot in gas and very little in electricity.
I have used a good deal of both.
Does the minister mean to tell this committee that gas is cheaper than electric power ?
Yes.
Then why is so much electric power being developed ? There is not a man in this Dominion but who believes that gas is dearer than electric power; otherwise it would be used. *
I can .tell the hon. gentleman that in the citv of St. John, I used gas before I had my house wired for electricity. I am satisfied that electric light cost me twice what gas had formerly cost.
We are speaking of Ottawa, and not St. John. I do not know anything about St. John, but I know that power in Ottawa is sold at probably $15 per horse-power.
No.
Well, others can get it if the minister can not. Any manufacturing industry in Ottawa that wants power, can get it for that.
You may get it undeveloped at the dam for $15.

That is what it is any place. In Ottawa it is only $15 or $20 per horse-power. I would like the minister to explain how it is that he is now spending $53,000 for lighting these buildings, when it only cost $24,000 when gas was used. If that goes on each year, where are we going to end? I would like the minister to tell the committee one single item in regard to which he has decreased the expenditure or effected economies since he became minister. Can he name one single instance ? If he does, I -will guarantee to name several where he has increased the expenditure a good deal more, and in connection with these increases, I believe that there has been grafting, robbery and that kind of thing going on. Will the minister name one ?
We are just at the present time discussing the lighting of the buildings throughout Canada.
I am speaking of Ottawa.

Neither in respect of these buildings nor in respect of the lighting of the buildings in the city of Ottawa, can I show a decrease for the reason that every year the number of rooms which is being occupied for the different departments of the government is increasing. Since 1896 there have been a great many hands, possibly a thousand, of clerks added to the different departments for the purpose of attending to the expanding business of the country. My hon. friend has heen asleep during the past fourteen years, he does not know that the country has been growing with marvellous rapidity, that its business has doubled, almost trebled in that period of time. The hon. gentleman forgets all that.
The clerks have, but the business has not.

Beyond the buildings which were occupied in 1896, we have two large buildings on Slater street, the large building on Bank street, the building on O'Connor street, the building on Queen street, and the Corry building, near the railway station. All these buildings are occupied in addition to those which were occupied in 1896. They have to be lighted and that adds to the expense. We have additional charges for gas and electricity. But let my hon. friend go any day to the committee on Public Accounts, when experts are there who know these things, and find out whether we are spending for them one single dollar more than we ought to spen'd.	.
We have had that in the Public Accounts Committee.

Will the minister deny that wdien this fraud was exposed in the Public Accounts Committee last year the committee practically unanimously agreed that it should be condemned and the minister cancelled the contract and admitted he had not made a good bargain. How would it be possible for the Public Accounts Committee to investigate every item of the expenditure of $100,000,000. I appeal now to the Alinister of Finance because I believe he wants to help these items through and desires to see honest expenditure. The Alinister
of Finance must know that there was rascality shown up in the Public Accounts Committee, and I would ask him, as I asked the Alinister of Public Works this afternoon, to appoint Judge Cassels a commissioner to investigate the Public Works Department, just as he investigated the Alarine and Fisheries Department. Judge Cassels' report would satisfy not only the members on this side but the public of Canada generally. Of course when I preferred this request to the Minister of Public Works he raised the objection that everythingvhad been straight and that we had not shown any wrong-doing. The Deputy Alinister of Finance is present at every meeting of the Public Accounts Committee watching the proceedings, and I am satisfied the Minister of Finance will not stand up here to-night and declare that everything has been found straight and right in the Public Works Department. I think the Alinister of Finance will admit that we have proven that rascality and graft has been going on in that department. Would it not be in the interest of the public to have the Minister of Finance grant a commission of inquiry? Should he do so, speaking for myself, I am satisfied the members of this side would cheerfully let the items go through, if we were promised an investigation by Judge Cassels, an upright and honourable man who is in no way connected with the members on this side of the House. Cannot the Minister of Finance grant that simple and reasonable request and let us see how it will work out? I appeal to him to do so.

That was the defence always g'veu by the government, that there was nothing the matter with the government; everything was all right. But when a commission investigated the department it found that there was no conscience in that department at all. It is useless for us to go over the condemnation meted out to the government by gentlemen appointed by themselves to investigate one department. Mv hon. friend has the same excuse now. The Alinister

of Public Works said there was nothing wrong, that no investigation was required, and the Minister of Finance states: Whatever the Minister of Public Works said this afternoon I will endorse. That shows the great faith the Minister of Finance has in the Minister of Public Works. It is well known that the people of Canada are not satisfied with the various departments. Something went wrong with the department of the Secretary of State (Mr. Murphy). I am not charging him, because I suppose most of the wrong-doing occurred before he assumed that position, but that hon. gentleman said that the investigation in the Printing Bureau proved the country had lost $70,000 by irregularities in the department. These are the things that have' .aToused suspicions in the country. The hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Reid) has asked for a general investigation into the Public Works Department. If there is nothing wrong in that department my hon. friend will not suffer. One department had to bring bookkeepers from New York at a cost of $50 and $75 a day per man and expenses to look into the bookkeeping of the department. I thought that Canada was as well versed in bookkeeping as the United States, but the minister was careful not to allow any Canadian to look into that department. He said in effect that there was nobody in Canada equal to the occasion. They found all this wrong-doing. The opposition now want an investigation into my hon. friend's department. Why not have a general investigation, which will avoid all this detailed criticism?
