These are some of the wrong-doings that have been found by the investigations made by this side of the House and by gentlemen appointed by this government. The hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Reid) is asking for the appointment of a public commission to investigate this department generally, avoiding these detailed investi-Mr. BLATN.
gations here, a commission which will be able to lift the lid when the government are not there to hold it down. I thought the minister was going to accede to that request, but I misjudged him, as I have done before. I hope now, that having heard this statement of willingness from this side to assist him in satisfying the public, who are rather suspicious of my hon. friend's department, perhaps not suspicious of himself, he will grant the commission. Tonight we asked to have public competition in the supply of light. He says: Oh, no, that is against the policy of my government; we do not want public competition. We want to ask people to give prices, and he says he is a little fearful lest we shall get a lower price than the private individual. If the minister grants an investigation and it is found that there is nothing wrong he will have support in the future from this side that he cannot have now, when his department is surrounded by suspicion.

I am surprised the minister did not state whether he believed there .had been anything wrong in the Public Works Department. He must have got information from his deputy minister, and these facts must have been brought to his attention. The very item we are on was before the Public Accounts Committee last year, and I would ask whether the minister heard the result of that investigation? At the same time last year there was another investigation about a firm in Montreal, the Lymburner firm. The minister must admit that that firm was getting about 200 per cent profit. Every one on this side expected that when it was shown that that firm was charging such prices the Public Works Department would cease doing business with them, but to our surprise we again find the name in the accounts of this year. On finding the high prices charged by this film we got the accounts and we found that the goods were bought from Lymburner, and certified by a man named Lymburner. We brought him here and found that he was a shareholder and director of the company from whom the department were buying these goods, receiving money as dividends from the firm from which he was buying goods as agent of the department-and he must have been receiving good big dividends, judging by the prices the government paid. He was appointed at $1,300 a year by the Public Works Department as inspector to certify that goods he was purchasing from his own company were correct and the prices fair and just. I would like to ask the Minister of Finance, who is leading the House tonight, and should answer, if he considers-

WTould the hon. gentleman allow me to ask him a question? Were not tenders and prices asked for from

two or three different firms, and was not the tender of Lymburner, Limited, the lowest?
The way in which these tenders were asked for
Please answer my question.
As far as my memory serves me, the Lymburner, Limited, were not the lowest tenderers.
The hon. gentleman's memory does not serve him rightly because they were.

In the matter referred to, public tenders were not called for. There was a letter purporting to contain a tender sent by the firm of Millen & Thom, for the sum of $520 for repairs to be done a certain elevator in the .old examining warehouse in Montreal, the exact date of which letter I have forgotten. But ten days later another letter came from the firm of Lymburner, Limited, tendering for. the same work for the sum of $506.50, which was immediately accepted. These were the only tenders received; but according to the evidence of both the Lymburners there were 20 firms in Montreal capable of performing the same kind of work.' Under those circumstances it is perfectly just and right to say that no tenders were called. Even if it could be said that tenders were called, the evidence on the face of it would go to show there was collusion.

After a statement of this kind, does the Minister of Finance think it unreasonable that we should ask for an investigation? Is he willing that irregularities of this kind should be allowed to continue in any public department and' the finances of this country wasted in this manner? This is only one sample, we have named others, and if the Minister of Finance wants more we can give them. I would like him to say if, from the investigations which have taken place in the Public Accounts Committee and from what he has heard in this House, he thinks that everything has been going on right in the Department of Public Works. If not will he give us this one chance to show the real condition of affairs; and if the Public Works Department can show a clean sheet after such an investigation, we shall be quite willing to let the Department of the Secretary of State and the others go scot free. If the hon. the Minister of Finance is not afraid to speak, he ought to have no hesitatibn in giving a reply.

With respect to the transaction referred to by the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes') I beg to remind the committee that the circumstances were not all disclosed in my hon. friend's statement. Mr. Lymburner, the inspector, said that he sent out four different notices to parties engaged in that kind of work, that he received only two tenders, and that the contract was awarded to the lowest. And Mr. Lymburner has stated that he had ceased to be a director of the company the moment he became an employee of the 1 department.
On the contrary, the evidence on oath of that gentleman was that he is still a director and has been since the incorporation of the company.
A shareholder.
And a director.
He had been at one time the managing director.
And is still a director.
And is still a stockholder of the company.
And a director.

Furthermore it was disclosed that the work was done at the lowest cost at which such work could be done in Montreal. Nor was there any attempt made by the hon. member for Cumberland, who was conducting the investigation, to prove any overcharge. I am .confident that the evidence when reported to the House, will disclose that the work was done at the lowest price obtainable and that Mr. Lymburner had certified that he had no other interests in that company than that of a stockholder.

This incident is an illustration of the old saying that the unexpected generally hannen's. The result of this discussion has been, in my judgment, to give us in the last fifteen minutes the most important announcement made on the floor of parliament in the last 15 years. Ever since 1896, we have been taught to look on the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) as the watchdog of the treasury, the one man in the cabinet whose honesty was to be depended upon to prevent the squandering of public money in the departments of colleagues less scrupulous than himself. To-night, however, the Minister of Finance repudiated the idea that at any time he was ever the guardian of the treasury and states that he is merely the receptacle of the opinions of his colleagues. If anv one of his colleagues says: ' Everything is right in my department ' then, according to the Minister of Finance, his sole duty is to accept it. Now, I have either correctly or incorrectly given the statement made by my hon. friend. There is no member of this House who would be less willing than myself to misrepresent him in any way: and if I have in any degree misunderstood and consequently misrepresented his statement,

320S
I shall with pleasure give way and allow him to correct the understanding I took from the statement he made on the floor of this House.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not quarrelling with the hon. gentleman's version of what I said. My statement will appear in ' Hansard ' and will speak for itself and I am willing to be judged by it.

Unfortunately it is impossible for us to have the ' Hansard ' report at this moment, but every hon. gentleman present who heard the statement made will judge the Finance Minister by it, no matter what ' Hansard ' may say. I say that the statement he made when appealed to by my hon. friend from Grenville (Mr. Reid) to consent to an investigation into certain departments on the grounds alleged by my hon. friend, namely, that the conditions, the transactions and the figures of these departments justified investigation-when that appeal was made, the Minister of Finance had but one answer. That answer was this:	I have been told
by my colleagues that these figures ars correct. Am I right or wrong in that statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman says he does not care what ' Hansard ' may sav. I do. ' Hansard ' will report what happened, and I am content to be judged by it.

I agree with every word that ' Hansard ' says to-morrow ; but I am speaking of the present, of to-night, and I am speaking in the presence of hon. members who heard the statement made by the Minister of Finance. And what do we in this House care for what ' Hansard ' may say to-morrow? Does the hon. gentleman expect that the unrevised version of ' Hansard ' will give a different statement from that which rang in the ears of every hon. member of this House a few moments ago? What about this reference to 'Hansard'? Either ' Hansard ' will ibe correct or it will not. If it be correct, it will IBear out the statement I have made. If it does not, I say it will be incorrect, and I speak in the hearing of those who heard the hon. gentleman. I say that the hon. gentleman, when appealed to as ' the watchdog of the treasury,' repudiated responsibility as watchdog-he is not even an alarm clock ; it is for him merely to accept the accounts handed in by his colleagues. ' Hansard,' I hope, will report my words as well as those of the Minister of Finance. But the crucial matter is that this House has, for the first time in its history, heard a Minister of Finance deliberately state on this floor that he practically has no responsibility whatever for the accounts of his colleagues so long as they tell him those Mr. NORTHRUP.
accounts are correct. And think of a minister of Finance who is the only man out of two hundred and twenty members of this House who does not know that the accounts have not been correct for years gone by ! Can any man possibly have attended the meetings of the Public Accounts Committee, year after year-and I have seen the Minister of Finance there-when accounts were investigated and not know that accounts "were brought before this House that were not correct? Yet the Minister of Finance, knowing that these accounts are not correct, is prepared, in the face of this House and before Heaven, to say_ that he has no further responsibility to this House and to the people of Canada than to accept any statement made to him by any of his colleagues. The question before the House is a comparatively small matter, a mere question of expenditure. But I think the House is to be congratulated that, in the discussion of this comparatively small matter, we have had enunciated by the Minister of Finance a principle which the people of this country will understand and remember-that, since the year 1896, there has not been anybody in charge of the Department of Finance, and that the minister had no responsibility to anybody in this country except his colleagues. We understand now why the Farmers Bank was chartered.
There are other people in Canada who made the request of this government to have further investigation of these departments, including the Department of Public Works.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain) wishes to continue the argument on that line, I have to remind him that the item before us is that of lighting the Dominion buildings at Ottawa. Unless the arguments can be made somewhat applicable to that subject, I cannot allow the discussion to take a wider range.

I obey your decision, Mr. Chairman. We are discussing the. question whether there should be an investigation of this lighting or not, and whether an investigation should be by this House spending hour after hour upon it, or whether it should he by commission. And I was pointing out that other people have suggested that a thorough and public investigation should be made, and this I substantiate by reading a statement of the commissioners who investigated the Marine Departmext :
Your commissioners regret having been unable to investigate the condition of things in some of the other departments. But to do the work with any pretensions to thoroughness would take much more time than would probably be agreeable to the government.

That is the statement of gentlemen appointed toy the government to investigate one department. If they had reached the department having this lighting in charge, I suppose they would have said they regretted they had not an opportunity to go into still other departments. To have matters of this kind cleared up and to allay public suspicion, this side of the House moved a resolution asking for an investigation into all large spending departments which would include the lighting contracts. I need not put this resolution again on ' Hansard;' the Minister of Finance remembers it well, and so does the Minister of Public Works. In the face of that statement by gentlemen appointed by themselves, that other departments required investigation, we on this side put ourselves on record as asking for a thorough investigation of the Public Works Department and others. This was moved in 1909. And what did the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Public Works do? Why, they recorded their votes against the resolution, declaring that, no matter what the commissioners said, they found no wrong-doing in the Marine and Fisheries Department and suggested in their report that there is wrong-doing in other departments and regret very much that they had not the opportunity to investigate it.
They did not say, I think, that there was wrong-doing in other departments.

That is what they said :
Your commissioners regret having been unable to investigate the condition of things in some of the other departments.
The hon. gentleman said that they reported that there was wrongdoing in the other departments.
What else would he take out of it?
I would not take out of it what the hon. gentleman (Air. Blain) stated.
If the hon. minister feels that everything is right in his department, why refuse the investigation?
No necessity for it.

The hon. member for West Lamtoton (Mr. Pardee) said, before the investigation, that there was nothing wrong in the Marine Department. But his friends the commissioners said there was something wrong and that the department had no conscience. But the point- is that we are asking that in such matters as this lighting contract there should be an investigation. A year ago we asked for a commission of investigation, and I was much surprised that the Minister of Finance should vote against it. I had a great deal
more confidence in him, and I thought he had more confidence in the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) than there would seem to have been at that time.
They got into trouble with one commission, and they did not want any more.

Exactly. Suppose the opposition were to move for an investigation into my hon. friend's (Mr. Pugsley's) department, where would he stand? Has he the same policy now? He has learned some new things, I am sure. We have had him before the Public Accounts Committee, for instance, on the sawdust wharf. He knows the weak points of that wharf as well as the strong ones. And the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) knows it too. That wharf is in the eastern part of Canada, and he is always anxious to protect the eastern part.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend's (Mr. Blain) friends- in eastern Canada never give me that credit.

I do not know what credit the minister has, but I know what he does; when we ask for investigation he refuses not only by speech but by vote. I suppose we are to go on without public competition for lighting for my hon. friend is opposed to investigation, and to public competition. Therefore, the friends of this government must be fed with contracts. When the Minister of Public Works is asked as to competition, he says: We have a list, and we ask those upon the list to tender. One hon. gentleman has shown that there were twenty people ready to tender. Why did not the minister put the whole twenty on the list, or, better still, advertise publicly, thus brushing away all suspicion with regard to his department that the public interest is not maintained?

There is no list, I think, but Mr. Lymburner said his authority was to buy from anybody at the cheapest possible rate, and he thought he had secured sufficient competition by these circulars.
Power for running elevators, stamp-cancelling machines, &c., $32,000.
This is an increase of $7,000 owing to the increase in the number of buildings throughout the country.
We ought to have some information as to where these are.

This is to provide for the cost of electric power for running elevators and other machines in the public buildings throughout the Dominion. It is estimated that the power for elevators now installed will cost $25,820, and for those being installed $4,320. I cannot give further details, because these are simply buildings tlmoughout the whole Dominion.
COMMON >3
What course does the minister pursue in towns where there are two lighting plants, as, for instance, in the city of Brantford?
I am sure that what we do is to get the lowest price from the companies, but we do not advertise for tenders.
Why not? Are you afraid you will get it too cheap?

We could not possibly get it cheaper than we do. My horn, friend knows that these companies have just two rates, a flat rate, and a meter rate, and whichever of these rates is applied it is the same to everybody.
Why not call for tenders?
We could not get a reduced rate.
The minister has not tried.

I know perfectly well we could not do it. I have here a list of these buildings throughout the Dominion for which this $32,000 is estimated. It takes in the parliament buildings and many other buildings in Ottawa, and the public buildings in many cities throughout the Dominion.
What is the fixed rate for power?
The average rate is about $30 per annum per horse-power.
A pretty high rate.
Not at retail, I think.
The minister speaks of there being only the flat rate, and the meter rate. And, if I understood him correctly, he gave the flat rate as $2.25 a lamp.
The company rate here in Ottawa is $2.25 per lamp for the first three thousand lamps, and $2 after that? From the city we get a straight rate of $2.

The minister said that is as low a rate as he could expect. How-does he account for the fact that in the town of Orillia they sell at $2 per lamp even if a man takes only four or five necessary to light a small house? Speaking with the mayor of Orillia, he told me that they were paying expenses and making a good profit besides; they did not require that the consumer should take 2,000 or 3,000 lamps before getting the benefit of this rate.
Do I understand that a man can get'enough to light a small house for $8 a year-four lights at $2 apiece?

Yes. And I have known it to be as low as $1 a year. But I think that that is below the Tate at which it can be furnished to-day. But the point in this Mr. PUGSLEY.
case is the point of public competition. There are many places where competition is not possible, but there are other towns and cities that have two or three plants, and, in such cases, I regard it as the duty of the Minister of Public Works to ask for tenders. If that were done, no one could reasonably find fault; but, so long as he does otherwise, there is a suspicion that he has not done his whole duty.
Rents, &c., $260,000.

This is to make provision for payment of rents during the next fiscal year of buildings leased for the public departments in all parts of the Dominion. This takes in the whole of the Dominion including the city of Ottawa. Perhaps I might give the list to the committee: Nova Scotia, Halifax, examining warehouse $1,000; penitentiary 24 cents-I do not know what that means; North Sydney, engineer's office $120; Prince Edward Island, Charlottetown, engineer's office, $200; Grand Falls, post office, $120; St. John, customs house, water lots, $22; immigration detention building, $2,105.37; Quebec, $15,861; Ontario, $184,847; Manitoba $4,304; Saskatchewan, $7,487; Alberta, $11,760; British Columbia, $2,700; Peace River district $300. That makes- a total of $233,099.11. Then, for phones the total is $1,737.65.
I would like to ask the minister if the same generous rental is paid in outside places throughout the Dominion that is shown to be paid in the city of Ottawa?

Perhaps 1 might better answer that question in another way, by saying that the same economy is observed in the city of Ottawa as is observed throughout the Dominion, and if my hon. friend will take the rentals we are paying throughout the Dominion for accommodation for custom houses and post offices I think he will see that we are very prudent and economical; in fact, some people may-say that we are too much so.
Dominion buildings, salaries of engineers, Bremen, caretakers, &e., $235,000.

This is for the purpose cf paying salaries in Ottawa and throughout the Dominion. I have a list for the different provinces of the engineers and caretakers and their salaries. I will not read it to the committee, because it would take several hours, but if any hon. gentleman wishes to inquire as to ahy particular matter I will be very glad to give him the information.
I would like to hear about Manitoba.

I will give the information to my hon. friend with pleasure. In Manitoba we have 32 engineers, firemen

and caretakers to whom we pay $23,366, or that is the estimate of their salaries for the coming year.
Are these engineers employed entirely in public buildings?
In public buildings.
Not on dredges?
No. .
About what figure do you pay your caretakers in these buildings?

In Amherst we pay $400; Annapolis, $400; Antigonish, $400; Arichat, $150; Baddeck, $250; Bridgewater, $400; Glace Bay, $600; Halifax, $750. I think we pay a little more when we get west of Lake Superior. At Winnipeg we pay the engineer at the old post office $960; firemen, $720; elevator man, $650; electrician, $1,080, and so on.

Are these certificated engineers?
Mr. PUGSLEYL The engineers are all certificated, but the caretakers are not.
Dominion cattle quarantine stations, renewals, repairs, &c., $20,000.
That amount is required by the Department of Agriculture.
I think we ought to have the Department of Agriculture here to explain it.

This vote is required to make provision for the construction of corrals and dipping vats along the boundary line between Canada and the United States, and the maintenance of cattle quarantine stations generally throughout the Dominion in a proper state of repair and efficiency during the fiscal year ending March 30, 1912. The whole is in accordance with a request made by the Deputy Minister of Agriculture. He has written a letter in which he urges that this amount should be placed in the estimates.
How many of these dipping stations does he propose to build along the boundary?

He has not given the information as to those. Perhaps my hon. friend will be good enough to allow me to get the Minister of Agriculture to give him the information when his estimates are under consideration.
I am not objecting to the item, but we would like to know what they are doing in other lines, because some people think there is a good deal of danger of importing disease.
We have these stations in a number of places in the different provinces.
What do each of these stations cost ?
From $500 to $600 each. We may have to erect one on an emergency and a vote has to be available. I will get the particulars for my hon. friend when the agricultural items are under consideration.
We are running business without a quorum, and I am afraid I will have to draw the attention of the chairman to it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There are 20 members present.
It will be distinctly understood that when the agricultural estimates are up, we will get all the information about this vote ?

That is clearly understood.
Yukon public buildings, $75,000.
We ought to have some information about this. The population is constantly decreasing and the expenses are about the same.

I have the details here as to the cost for each building. 'We have been paying Mr. Bertrand, agent for the department, a salary of $4,000. He is clerk of works or superintendent of buildings, but he is leaving the Yukon and i think he intends resigning his position. If so, one of the other officials will discharge the duties of the office and it will not be necessary to fill Mr. Bertrand's place. There is a reduction of $5,000 on this vote.
Are you providing for a salary of $4,000 for that office next year?
The total vote is reduced by $5,000. We will not have Mr. Bertrand's salary to pay, although we may have to pay some other official a slight increase for looking after the woTk.
That is not what I asked. Are you providing for a salary of $4,000 for the man who fills this office ?

I am unable to tell my hon. friend without going into details. The result is a total of $5,000 less than last year. One official, Mr. Bertrand, has resigned, and we expect to have his duties performed by another official, possibly at some increase in salary.
That does not give the slightest information in regard to his salary. Does it account for the reduction of $5,000?

What is the population now?
321a
I do not know exactly. It has declined from the boom days, but there is considerable permanent mining, hydraulic mining, and, I think, in some parts of the district, quartz mining.
The department is expending a good deal there?

Yes, but we are making reductions. The services of quite a number of officials in the Interior Department have been dispensed with, and we are dispensing with the services of one of our most heavily salaried men.
Is the post office building for which there is a vote of $13,000 a government owned building?
Yes.
How many employees are there?
There is a caretaker at $160 a month, a night caretaker at $160, a charwoman, and then this vote includes' the lighting service, fuel,, water and scavenger service, &c.
Would the postmaster live in the building?
I have no memorandum on that point, but I assume not, because I presume the caretaker lives there.

A very commonplace man who is reliable will do quite well as a caretaker, and here you are paying two men at the rate of $1,920 each per annum. In many post offices in the east the caretakers live in the building and receive very small salaries. Formerly, we paid very high salaries in the Yukon and were told it was owing to the high cost of living, but that the expenses were coming down. I should think that you could get good, useful, reliable men to do the work there for one-half the money.

I would not think so; that would be about what we pay in Winnipeg. In the Yukon the conditions are not pleasant and wages and expenses are very high, so that for these positions we have to pay good salaries. I do not think we could get reliable caretakers in the Yukon for less than we are paying. In the east we get them in many cases for $400 or $250, but in the west we have to pay more and in the Yukon we have found it impossible to get reliable caretakers for less than we pay.
Do they reside in the building or not?
I can obtain a memorandum of that from the department.

I heard it stated recently that the population of the Yukon is Mr. BLAIN.
now between 2,000 and 3,000 people. Some years ago we were told the population was 20,000 people from all over the world, and that it was necessary to keep a large staff there at high salaries, because of the unsettled condition of things there' and the danger c/i the turbulent element. We are told that we have to pay them very high figures because everything is very dear there, but the population, has been growing less and the revenues have been diminishing, and there is no reason why the numbers of this force should not be diminished. Yet we keep up the same number from year to year, and every year we are given the same reasons, namely, that it is necessary in the interests of peace and safety to keep up the number. Yet we are told by men from Dawson that that city is just as peaceful as Toronto or Montreal. Why there should not be a greater reduction I do not understand.

The country is very remote, and it is difficult to get into it and out of it. In the winter you have to take a journey of a good many miles until you strike the railway at Whitehorse. It is a part of the country where people do not like to live, unless attracted by mining and work incidental to that industry. I do not think it would be possible to get caretakers for less than we are paying these. The suggestion of my hon. friend that we should reduce the number of employees is however, worthy of consideration. The department of the Interior has made considerable deductions. We are dispensing with the services of one of our highest priced men, who has resigned, because he got tired of living out there.
Have you given him any other office ?
Not so far as my department is concerned.
In any other department ?
Not that I am aware of. That will make a saving of $4,000 very nearly. He was clerk of works and superintendent of buildings and general agent of the government in connection with expenditures.

I have no objection to paying good salaries and I quite understand that the conditions out there are peculiar, but it would be well for the minister to look into this question and see how it is this building requires so many employees. $13,000 seems a pretty large amount apart from the other salaries paid.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I had the privilege the summer before last of spending 10 days in Dawson City. The public building contains the post office, customs house and

Inland revenue office, and quite a number of officials are housed there. Dawson is one of the most important post offices in the Dominion, from the fact that large quantities of gold are sent through it.
But what have the caretakers to do -with that ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: These caretakers probably also act as night and day watchmen. I think they do not live in the building, as there did not appear to be room there for them, and their salaries, when we consider the enormous cost of living out there, are not large. Half of that salary in the city of Ottawa, would be very high, compared witiv the full amount out in the Yukon. Of course the population of Dawson has been decreasing, but I think it has arrived at the point now where the decrease will cease, especially as hydraulic mining is increasing and large companies are in operation there. In my department there, the inspector of weights and measures gets a salary of $2,500 and he may possibly resign because he claims he cannot live there on that figure.
I can quite understand a man like that requiring to be extra'well paid, but I do not see that a caretaker is at all in the same category.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: These may not be ordinary caretakers, but watchmen and very capable men.

A caretaker is simply there to look after the building. Even though he cannot write his name, he may be more reliable than many a B.A. You can often find a man working as a road-maker, or drain-digger, who is as reliable as the most highly educated man you could choose. It is not fair to compare the inspector of weights and measures with the caretaker of a building. We get little information from the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Templeman) when we ask whether this man lives in the building.
I understand the minister to say he does not.
No, he does not state that.
I think he does.
I must accept the evidence of my own ears rather than the recollection of the Minister of Public Works.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I said that from my inspection of the building my impression was that he did not live in the building- there was no Toom.

We have heard it stated here that a rent of $40 a month for living quarters in any ordinary public building would be a reasonable figure. If a man were living there and had a family he would have his rent free, and, even counting this at $20, it would be a considerable sum which should be taken into account. And there is also his fuel, light and other things which add a good deal. We have not known whether these caretakers get these perquisites or not. Comparing with what is paid for this class of men throughout the country generally, it would seem that we pay a high figure. I know that for years we have been paying high salaries out there. The minister says they are trying to reduce them as well as they can. In
1909-	10 the expenditure was $80,000, in
1910-	11 it was the same, and in 1911-12 the estimate is $75,000, a reduction of $5,000.
Could the minister, on a future day, give us the total expenditure and total revenue of the Yukon?
That covers more than my department, and I would suggest that the hon. gentleman should move for a return.
If the hon. gentleman is unwilling-
I am willing to give anything in my own department.
Will the hon. gentleman give the total revenue and expenditure of the Yukon in his own department?

I will make a note of that.
Some resolutions reported.
